governingPrinciple: Act first. Learn more when needed.

medicalDisclaimer: First-aid instructions support immediate bystander care and do not replace professional emergency medical assessment, diagnosis, or hospital treatment. Call 911 in any life-threatening emergency.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Check that the scene is safe before approaching, then check responsiveness, breathing, and severe bleeding.
recognitionSigns: Someone appears ill, injured, collapsed, or distressed
Unclear whether a life-threatening condition is present
Person does not react normally to voice or touch (AVPU less than Alert)
steps: Scan the surroundings for danger (traffic, fire, electricity, gas, water, or violence) before approaching.
Approach calmly in the person's line of sight, introduce yourself, and ask what happened.
Check responsiveness if motionless: gently shake the shoulders (or tap a baby's foot) and ask loudly, 'Are you alright?'
Open the airway if unresponsive (tilt head back and lift chin; neutral head position for a baby) and check for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds.
Check quickly for life-threatening external bleeding and press firmly on any severe bleed.
Call 911 immediately using speakerphone if the person is unresponsive, breathing abnormally, or bleeding severely, and treat the most urgent threat first.
Leave a responsive person in the position most comfortable for them unless you must move them from immediate danger, and monitor until help arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is unresponsive and NOT breathing normally (or only gasping)
conditionalActions.action: Start CPR immediately and send someone for an AED.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is unresponsive and breathing normally with no suspected spinal injury
conditionalActions.action: Roll them onto their side in the recovery position to keep the airway open.

conditionalActions.condition: If cross-infection (respiratory epidemic) is suspected
conditionalActions.action: Assess breathing visually by watching chest or abdominal movement without placing your face near theirs.

warnings: Do not approach an unsafe scene you cannot make safe; call emergency authorities from a safe distance.
Do not move a seriously injured person unless they are in immediate danger or their position prevents life-saving airway care.
Do not film an emergency scene; protect the person's privacy and keep paths clear for responders.
emergencyEscalation: Unresponsiveness or anything less than fully Alert on the AVPU check
Absent, noisy, gasping, or difficult breathing
Severe external bleeding or signs of circulatory shock
Suspected heart attack, stroke, poisoning, anaphylaxis, or spinal trauma

learnMore.overview: A systematic initial assessment (primary survey or DR ABC: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation) helps first aiders quickly identify and treat life-threatening conditions in order of urgency while staying safe.
causes: Sudden medical emergencies (cardiac arrest, stroke, anaphylaxis, hypoglycemia)
Traumatic injuries (falls, road crashes, severe bleeding, burns)
Environmental hazards or acute psychological distress
riskFactors: Bystander hesitation or uncertainty ('bystander effect') delaying early care
Dynamic hazards at road, industrial, water, or disaster scenes
detailedRecognition: AVPU scale: Alert (eyes open spontaneously, follows instructions), Verbal (responds only to voice), Pain (reacts only to gentle pinch/squeeze), Unresponsive (no reaction).
If a person can speak or cry clearly, their airway is open and breathing is currently adequate.
Altered mental status (confusion, drowsiness, uncharacteristic aggression) signals a potentially serious condition.
prevention: Keep emergency numbers (911, Red Cross 143) saved and accessible.
Maintain a stocked first aid kit at home, school, and work.
preparation: Practise using phone speakerphone mode so you can call EMS and give care simultaneously.
Remember that lack of formal equipment should never stop life-saving actions like CPR or direct pressure with clean cloth.
explanations: Addressing breathing and severe bleeding first preserves oxygen delivery to the brain and heart during the critical minutes before EMS arrives.
Calm eye-level communication reduces panic and helps both physical and emotional stabilization.
additionalPrecautions: Ask consent before examining a responsive person and explain each step before touching them.
Prioritize connecting injured or distressed children with their parents or caregivers.
followUpCare: Hand over clear observations to EMS, including when symptoms started, changes noticed, and any prescribed medication taken.
Check in on your own well-being after responding to a distressing emergency.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stop and scan for hazards to yourself, the injured person, and bystanders before approaching.
recognitionSigns: Fire, smoke, downed power lines, unstable structures, or oncoming traffic
Deep or fast-moving water, confined spaces, chemical spills, or toxic fumes
Violence, weapons, or severely agitated behaviour
Multiple injured people at the same incident
steps: Pause at a safe distance and identify any physical, chemical, electrical, water, or security hazards.
Eliminate or avoid hazards only if safe to do so; if the scene cannot be made safe, stay back and call 911 immediately.
Count how many people are injured and ask bystanders to call EMS, control crowds, or fetch an AED and first aid supplies.
Leave injured people where found unless an immediate danger forces you to move them to a safer spot.
Coach a responsive person verbally from a safe distance to apply self-care (such as pressing on a wound) if you cannot safely reach them.
Continuously re-check your surroundings as conditions, traffic, weather, or behaviour can change rapidly.

conditionalActions.condition: If multiple casualties are present
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 immediately to alert dispatchers, quickly assess everyone, and treat life-threatening breathing and severe bleeding problems first.

conditionalActions.condition: If an injured person MUST be moved from immediate danger
conditionalActions.action: Support their head, neck, and body alignment as best as possible and enlist another helper rather than lifting a seriously injured person alone.

conditionalActions.condition: If someone becomes violently agitated or threatening
conditionalActions.action: Maintain a safe distance, avoid physical contact, speak slowly and non-confrontationally if safe, and call security or police.

warnings: Never touch a person still in contact with live electricity or enter a gas-filled confined space without specialist rescue equipment.
Never pull a casualty from a vehicle after a crash unless fire, submerging water, or another immediate threat endangers their life.
Do not give unprescribed medication; only assist a person with their own prescribed emergency medicine when appropriate.
emergencyEscalation: Fire, explosion, electrical contact, chemical/gas exposure, or structural collapse
Road traffic collisions or multiple-casualty incidents
Violent threats, weapons, or unmanageable agitation

learnMore.overview: Protecting the responder, casualty, and bystanders is the first principle of every emergency. An injured responder cannot help others and adds another casualty to the incident.
causes: Environmental hazards (traffic, electricity, fire, water, extreme weather)
Hazardous materials or oxygen-poor confined spaces
Acute fear, head trauma, hypoxia, or substance effects causing agitation
riskFactors: Rushing toward a relative or friend without checking hazards
Bystander crowding or filming that blocks emergency responders
detailedRecognition: Look overhead, underfoot, and around the casualty for wires, fuel leaks, broken glass, or unstable debris.
Odourless gases like carbon monoxide or pooled carbon dioxide in cellars/tanks may cause multiple people to collapse in the same space.
prevention: Use high-visibility warning triangles or hazard lights at roadside incidents when safe.
Wear disposable gloves or improvise clean hand barriers (such as plastic bags) when handling blood.
preparation: Know local emergency numbers (911, Red Cross 143, local CDRRMO/BFP/PNP).
Learn where fire extinguishers, exits, first aid kits, and AEDs are located in schools and workplaces.
explanations: Unnecessary movement can worsen spinal fractures or internal bleeding, so casualties should only be moved when staying in place poses greater danger.
In multiple-casualty incidents, early EMS activation and prioritizing airway, breathing, and severe haemorrhage save the greatest number of lives.
additionalPrecautions: Inform EMS of any prescribed medication the person took or was assisted in taking.
Use bystanders constructively to form a privacy screen, create shade, or guide the ambulance.
followUpCare: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after the response and dispose of soiled dressings safely.
Seek peer or psychosocial support after witnessing severe or multi-casualty incidents.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Ensure physical safety first, then offer calm, non-intrusive support using Look, Listen, and Link.
recognitionSigns: Crying, trembling, numbness, confusion, or feeling overwhelmed during or after a crisis
Difficulty making decisions or meeting basic needs after an emergency
Unaccompanied children or distressed family members at an incident
steps: Look: Check for safety risks, physical injuries needing urgent first aid, urgent basic needs (water, warmth, shelter), and people in severe distress.
Approach calmly and respectfully at the person's eye level, introduce yourself, and offer a quiet, private space if possible.
Listen: Ask open, simple questions about what they need right now and listen attentively without judging or interrupting.
Reassure truthfully using a calm, soft voice and accept their emotions without pressuring them to talk about traumatic details.
Link: Help address practical needs (water, blanket, phone call), share clear factual updates, and connect them with family, friends, or community services.
Prioritize keeping children safe and reuniting them with their parents or trusted caregivers.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person does not want to talk or refuses support
conditionalActions.action: Respect their wishes without imposing help; let them know you or support services are nearby if needed.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person threatens self-harm, harm to others, or loses behavioural control
conditionalActions.action: Do not leave them alone if safe, keep the environment safe, and call 911 or mental health crisis services immediately.

warnings: Do not pressure anyone to recount details of a traumatic event or analyse their feelings.
Do not make false promises (reassure safety only when truthfully safe).
Remember that Psychological First Aid is humane practical support, not professional counselling or psychotherapy.
emergencyEscalation: Threats or attempts to harm themselves or others
Loss of behavioural control or unpredictable, destructive actions
Severe confusion, disorientation, or inability to sleep for a week
Inability to function or care for themselves or dependent children

learnMore.overview: Psychological First Aid (PFA) is a humane, supportive, and practical response to people experiencing acute distress during or after emergencies. Using the WHO/IFRC Look, Listen, Link cycle alongside physical first aid reduces stress and fosters recovery.
causes: Road crashes, sudden illness, injuries, fires, disasters, or violence
Witnessing resuscitation, injury, or loss of a loved one
riskFactors: Children separated from caregivers, older adults, and people with disabilities
Previous trauma, lack of social support, or prolonged crisis exposure
detailedRecognition: Acute stress reactions may be 'loud' (crying, shouting, restlessness) or 'silent' (numbness, withdrawal, staring).
Children react according to developmental age and how caregivers around them respond.
prevention: Protect privacy and dignity during physical first aid care.
Encourage healthy coping (rest, family connection, routines) and discourage harmful coping (alcohol/substance misuse, isolation).
preparation: Learn local health, social welfare, and mental health referral contacts.
Build personal self-care habits to prevent responder burnout.
explanations: Empowering people to make their own informed choices restores a sense of control after a disempowering crisis.
Connecting distressed individuals with loved ones and accurate information stabilizes anxiety and supports natural resilience.
additionalPrecautions: Ask permission before using comforting touch and respect cultural and gender norms.
Pause sensitive disclosures gently in group settings to protect privacy and prevent regret.
followUpCare: Follow up where appropriate to ensure referrals to medical, protection, or mental health services were reached.
Practise responder self-care (rest, peer check-ins, breathing exercises) after supporting others.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and clean running water for at least 20 seconds before and after giving non-urgent first aid.
recognitionSigns: Before and after caring for wounds, burns, eyes, or ill persons
Visibly soiled hands or after contact with blood, body fluids, dressings, or animals
steps: Wet your hands thoroughly with clean running water.
Apply soap and rub lather across all surfaces—palms, backs of hands, between fingers, thumbs, and under nails—for at least 20 seconds.
Rinse hands completely under clean running water.
Dry hands thoroughly with a clean towel or paper towel.
Dispose of used dressings, bandages, and gloves safely while protecting your hands, then wash hands immediately afterward.

conditionalActions.condition: If a life-threatening emergency requires immediate action (such as CPR or severe bleeding)
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT delay life-saving first aid to wash your hands; use gloves or a clean barrier if immediately at hand and wash thoroughly afterward.

conditionalActions.condition: If soap and clean water are unavailable and hands are not visibly soiled
conditionalActions.action: Rub alcohol-based hand gel (at least 70% ethanol or 60% other alcohol) over all hand and finger surfaces for at least 30 seconds until dry.

conditionalActions.condition: If neither soap nor sanitizer is available in a low-resource setting
conditionalActions.action: Clean ash may be used with water to rub and rinse hands.

warnings: Never delay urgent life-saving care because handwashing facilities are unavailable.
Wash hands even when disposable gloves were worn, as contamination can occur during glove removal.
Keep alcohol-based hand sanitizers out of reach of children under 6 years old.
emergencyEscalation: Accidental swallowing of hand sanitizer by a child (treat as Poisoning)
Needle-stick injury or high-risk blood exposure to broken skin, eyes, or mouth (seek medical evaluation)

learnMore.overview: Proper hand hygiene before and after first aid prevents the spread of bacteria and viruses between the responder and the ill or injured person. Soap and clean running water remain the gold standard.
causes: Direct transfer of bacteria, viruses, and fungi via unwashed hands or contaminated dressings
riskFactors: Open cuts on the responder's hands, long untrimmed fingernails, or touching wounds with dirty hands
Epidemic or pandemic outbreaks where respiratory and contact transmission are elevated
detailedRecognition: Critical handwashing times include before and after first aid, after toilet/diaper use, before handling food or eating, after coughing/sneezing, and after touching animals.
prevention: Keep fingernails short and trimmed.
Include disposable medical gloves and 70% ethanol (or >=60% isopropanol) hand rub in every first aid kit.
preparation: Practise safe glove removal (peeling inside-out without touching bare skin to the soiled exterior).
explanations: Rubbing soap lather for at least 20 seconds mechanically lifts microbes and oils so running water washes them away.
Alcohol hand rubs (>=70% ethanol or >=60% isopropanol/n-propanol) rapidly inactivate most bacteria and viruses when rubbed until dry (~30 seconds).
additionalPrecautions: Frequent alcohol sanitizer use can dry skin; glove-compatible moisturizer may be used to keep skin intact.
followUpCare: Monitor any wound exposed to unwashed contact for signs of infection (redness, warmth, swelling, pus, or fever).

quickInstructions.immediateAction: RESTRICTED TO TRAINED RESPONDERS: Untrained bystanders must NOT administer oxygen—call 911 and focus on airway, CPR, or positioning instead.
recognitionSigns: Trained provider identifies severe hypoxia (SpO2 <= 94% at sea level, or < 88% in known COPD)
Carbon monoxide poisoning, decompression illness, drowning with respiratory distress, or cardiac arrest during CPR
steps: Confirm you have completed specific oxygen-administration training and are legally permitted to give oxygen; otherwise do NOT attempt it.
Ensure the area is free of open flames, sparks, smoking, oil, or grease before opening oxygen equipment.
Call 911 first and never delay life-saving CPR, airway opening, or bleeding control to set up oxygen.

Administer supplementary oxygen via appropriate delivery device for indicated conditions: carbon monoxide exposure, decompression illness, drowning with breathing distress, cardiac arrest during CPR, or confirmed hypoxia.
Titrate oxygen to maintain SpO2 at 94% (or 88%–92% in confirmed COPD) if trained in pulse oximetry with a reliable medical-grade oximeter.
Discontinue or move high-flow oxygen away from the chest before delivering any defibrillator (AED) shock, and monitor continuously until EMS takes over.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person has a suspected stroke
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT give supplementary oxygen unless you are specifically trained and confirm the person is hypoxic.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person has cardiac chest pain
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT give routine oxygen; trained providers may give oxygen only if hypoxia is recognized, after calling EMS and assisting with aspirin.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person has confirmed COPD with life-threatening hypoxaemia (SpO2 < 88%)
conditionalActions.action: Do not withhold oxygen; titrate carefully toward 88%–92% when pulse oximetry is available.

warnings: Trained responders only: Routine or excessive oxygen (hyperoxia) can be harmful in stroke, heart attack, and COPD.
Never delay chest compressions or rescue breaths to attach supplementary oxygen.
Standard pulse oximeters give falsely normal readings in carbon monoxide poisoning and may overestimate SpO2 in darker skin tones.
Compressed oxygen is a severe fire/spark hazard—never defibrillate with high-flow oxygen blowing across the chest.
emergencyEscalation: Every condition requiring emergency supplementary oxygen requires immediate EMS activation (Call 911)

learnMore.overview: Supplementary oxygen is NOT a routine lay first aid measure. While critical in carbon monoxide poisoning, decompression illness, and hypoxic drowning, unnecessary oxygen can cause harm in non-hypoxic stroke or heart attack patients and requires specialized equipment training.
causes: Impaired gas exchange or oxygen transport (drowning, severe asthma, carbon monoxide poisoning, decompression illness, cardiac arrest)
riskFactors: Untrained use causing hyperoxia, CO2 retention in COPD, delayed CPR, or fire hazards
detailedRecognition: Physical assessment of breathing and responsiveness always takes priority over pulse oximeter readings.
Pulse oximetry can be inaccurate due to cold extremities, movement, nail polish, poor perfusion, darker skin pigmentation, or carbon monoxide.
prevention: Store and inspect compressed oxygen cylinders strictly according to regulatory safety rules away from heat and combustibles.
preparation: Complete certified oxygen administration and pulse-oximetry training if your responder role requires oxygen equipment.
explanations: Systematic reviews show routine oxygen does not improve survival in non-hypoxic myocardial infarction or stroke and high-flow oxygen increases mortality compared with titrated oxygen (88%–92%) in acute COPD exacerbations.
In carbon monoxide poisoning and decompression illness, high-concentration oxygen accelerates toxin/nitrogen clearance while awaiting hospital care.
additionalPrecautions: Vent any oxygen source at least 1 metre away and discontinue flow across the chest during AED shock delivery.
followUpCare: Report oxygen flow rate, delivery mask/cannula type, and start time to arriving EMS paramedics.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Place the person onto their side with their head tilted back (recovery position) to keep their airway open, and call 911.
recognitionSigns: Does not move, speak, or open eyes when you tap their shoulders (or tap a baby's foot) and speak loudly
Chest and abdomen rise and fall evenly with regular, quiet breaths (no gasping or gurgling)
steps: Check response by gently shaking the shoulders (or tapping a baby's foot) and asking loudly, 'Are you alright?'
Open the airway with the person on their back: gently tilt the head back (neutral position for a baby) and lift the chin.
Look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds.
Roll the person onto their side and tilt their head back so their airway stays open and fluids can drain (hold a baby on their side in your arms with head in a neutral position).
Call 911 immediately (use speakerphone if alone) and state that the person is unresponsive and breathing normally.
Watch their breathing continuously until EMS arrives, and look for clues to the cause (head injury, medical alert tag, diabetes, poisoning).

conditionalActions.condition: If breathing stops or becomes abnormal (gasping, irregular, or noisy)
conditionalActions.action: Roll them onto their back on a firm surface and start CPR immediately.

conditionalActions.condition: If you suspect a traumatic spinal injury
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT roll them unless the airway is blocked or EMS is far away and at least two helpers can turn them while keeping head, neck, and spine aligned; otherwise maintain an open airway using jaw thrust or gentle head-tilt chin-lift.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is visibly pregnant
conditionalActions.action: Place them in the recovery position on their LEFT side to avoid compressing major blood vessels.

warnings: Never leave an unresponsive person lying flat on their back unattended—relaxed muscles let the tongue fall back or vomit block the airway.
Never give food, water, or oral medication to an unresponsive person.
Do not confuse brief fainting (quick recovery) with ongoing unresponsiveness—always call 911 if they do not wake right away.
emergencyEscalation: Always call 911 immediately for any unresponsive person, even when breathing normally
Immediate escalation to CPR if breathing slows, gasps, or stops

learnMore.overview: An unresponsive person who is breathing normally cannot protect their own airway. Relaxed throat muscles allow the tongue to block airflow, and saliva, blood, or vomit can enter the lungs unless they are positioned on their side.
causes: Head injury, stroke, post-seizure state, diabetic emergency, poisoning, alcohol/drug intoxication, or hypoxia
riskFactors: Epilepsy, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, substance use, or head trauma
detailedRecognition: Normal breathing is regular, quiet, and effortless; irregular, noisy, or gasping (agonal) breaths indicate cardiac arrest requiring immediate CPR.
Using the AVPU scale, anyone responding only to Pain (P) or completely Unresponsive (U) needs airway protection and EMS.
prevention: Manage chronic conditions like diabetes or epilepsy according to medical plans and wear helmets/seatbelts.
preparation: Practise rolling an adult smoothly onto their side and holding an infant safely on their side with neutral head alignment.
explanations: Side-lying positioning uses gravity to keep the tongue forward and lets fluids drain freely from the mouth.
Left-lateral positioning in pregnancy prevents the uterus from compressing the inferior vena cava.
additionalPrecautions: Keep the person warm and protected from cold or wet ground while waiting for EMS.
followUpCare: Ensure medical evaluation even if the person wakes up before EMS arrives, to identify the underlying cause.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 (on speakerphone) and immediately push hard and fast in the centre of the chest at 100–120 compressions per minute.
recognitionSigns: Unresponsive (does not react to shoulder tap or loud voice)
Not breathing or only gasping / taking irregular, noisy breaths (agonal breathing)
steps: Shout for help and ask a bystander to call 911 and bring an AED; if alone, call 911 on speakerphone and begin CPR immediately.
Kneel beside the person on a firm surface and place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), with your other hand on top.
Keep your arms straight and push down approximately 5 cm (2 inches)—not deeper than 6 cm (2.4 inches)—at a steady rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
Allow the chest to rise completely after every push without leaning on the chest.

Combine 30 compressions with 2 rescue breaths (each breath over 1 second for visible chest rise, pausing compressions less than 10 seconds) if trained, able, and willing; otherwise continue uninterrupted chest compressions.
Attach and use an AED as soon as it arrives, following voice prompts and resuming compressions immediately after any shock.
Continue CPR without stopping (switching compressors every 2 minutes if another helper is present) until EMS takes over or the person wakes, moves purposefully, and breathes normally.

conditionalActions.condition: If cardiac arrest is due to drowning, choking, opioid overdose, or in an adolescent
conditionalActions.action: 30:2 CPR with rescue breaths is especially beneficial if you are able and willing to give breaths.

conditionalActions.condition: If respiratory infection transmission is suspected and you have no full PPE
conditionalActions.action: Perform continuous compression-only CPR, loosely cover the person's mouth and nose with a mask or cloth, and apply an AED as soon as possible.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is on a bed and moving them to the floor would delay care
conditionalActions.action: Start chest compressions immediately without delaying CPR, pressing firmly to compensate for mattress compression.

warnings: Do NOT check for a pulse—pulse checks by lay responders are unreliable and waste critical seconds.
Do NOT mistake occasional noisy gasps (agonal breathing) or brief initial seizure-like jerks for normal breathing—start CPR immediately.
If in doubt whether cardiac arrest is present, start CPR; the risk of serious harm to someone not in arrest is very low (<1%).
emergencyEscalation: Immediate 911 emergency call and urgent AED retrieval are required for every suspected cardiac arrest

learnMore.overview: Sudden cardiac arrest stops oxygen-rich blood from reaching the brain and vital organs within minutes. Immediate chest compressions pump blood manually and keep organs alive until an AED shock and emergency medical services can restore a normal heart rhythm.
causes: Heart attack (acute myocardial infarction) or sudden heart rhythm disturbance (most common in adults)
Asphyxial causes such as drowning, choking, severe asthma, trauma, or opioid overdose
riskFactors: Coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, or family history of sudden cardiac arrest
detailedRecognition: Apply adult/adolescent CPR to anyone who appears to have reached puberty.
Check normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds after head-tilt chin-lift; if unsure whether breathing is normal, treat as cardiac arrest.
prevention: Seek immediate EMS care for warning signs of cardiac chest pain before cardiac arrest occurs.
Manage cardiovascular risk factors and learn where public-access AEDs are installed.
preparation: Take hands-on or blended CPR and AED training with refresher practice every 3 to 6 months.
explanations: Pushing 5–6 cm deep at 100–120/min with full chest recoil maximizes blood flow to the heart and brain.
Rotating compressors every 2 minutes prevents rescuer fatigue from reducing compression depth.
Minimizing pauses (<10 seconds) maintains blood pressure needed for defibrillation to succeed.
additionalPrecautions: Use standard CPR hand placement and depth for obese adults and pregnant patients.
followUpCare: Even if the person regains consciousness and normal breathing after CPR or AED use, monitor closely until EMS arrives because cardiac arrest can recur.

source.topicTitle: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 (speakerphone) and start CPR combining chest compressions and rescue breaths immediately.
recognitionSigns: Child (about 1 year old up to puberty) does not respond to shoulder tap or loud voice
Not breathing or only gasping / taking irregular, noisy breaths
steps: Shout for help and ask a bystander to call 911 and get an AED; if alone with a phone, call 911 on speakerphone right away.
Place the child flat on their back on a firm surface, tilt the head back, lift the chin, and check for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds.
Place the heel of one hand (or two hands if the child is large or you are small) on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone).
Give 30 chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute, pressing one-third of the chest depth (approximately 5 cm / 2 inches) and allowing full recoil.
Open the airway (head-tilt chin-lift), pinch the child's nose, and give 2 steady mouth-to-mouth rescue breaths (1 second each, just enough to make the chest rise).

Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths (or 15:2 if you are a trained paediatric responder working with a second rescuer) until EMS takes over or the child breathes normally and moves purposefully.

conditionalActions.condition: If you are alone and have NO phone nearby to call on speakerphone
conditionalActions.action: Perform 1 minute of CPR first before briefly pausing to go call 911.

conditionalActions.condition: If you are unable or unwilling to give rescue breaths
conditionalActions.action: Give continuous chest-compression-only CPR at 100–120 compressions per minute without delay.

conditionalActions.condition: If an AED arrives
conditionalActions.action: Use a paediatric AED/pads for children under 8 years if available; if not, use a standard adult AED and pads without overlapping.

warnings: Do not check for a pulse—start CPR immediately if the child is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
Do not blow excessively hard or long during rescue breaths, as excess air inflates the stomach.
Rescue breaths are critically important in children because paediatric cardiac arrest usually starts from a breathing problem.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for every unresponsive child with absent or abnormal breathing

learnMore.overview: Unlike adults, cardiac arrest in children is most often caused by lack of oxygen from choking, drowning, asthma, or severe infection. Combining rescue breaths with chest compressions gives children a significantly better chance of survival and neurological recovery.
causes: Drowning, foreign-body choking, severe asthma or respiratory infection, trauma, or poisoning
riskFactors: Unsupervised water access, small choking hazards, or untreated severe respiratory distress
detailedRecognition: Treat anyone from roughly 1 year old until signs of puberty as a child; treat post-pubertal youth using Adult & Adolescent CPR.
Agonal gasps (slow, noisy, laboured gasps) are a sign of cardiac arrest, not normal breathing.
prevention: Supervise children closely around water, secure household poisons, and seek early care for severe breathing difficulty.
preparation: Note that both ventilation-first (2–5 initial breaths then 30:2) and compression-first (30:2) starts are acceptable in IFRC/ILCOR guidelines—starting immediately without delay matters most.
explanations: Observational studies in children aged 1–17 show higher survival and neurological recovery when rescue breaths are combined with chest compressions compared with compression-only CPR.
Using one or two hands adapts force to the child's chest size to achieve one-third chest depth (~5 cm) without rescuer fatigue.
additionalPrecautions: Switch compressors every 1 to 2 minutes with minimal pause if two providers are present.
followUpCare: Continue close monitoring until EMS takes over even if the child regains responsiveness and normal breathing.

source.topicTitle: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 (speakerphone) and immediately start infant chest compressions (4 cm deep) and gentle mouth-to-mouth-and-nose rescue breaths.
recognitionSigns: Baby (under 1 year) is limp, abnormal in colour, and does not react when picked up or tapped on the sole of the foot
Not breathing or only gasping / breathing irregularly
steps: Shout for help and ask someone to call 911 and bring an AED; if alone with a phone, call 911 on speakerphone immediately.
Place the baby flat on their back on a firm surface, tilt the head gently into a neutral 'sniffing' position (do NOT tilt far back), lift the chin, and check breathing for up to 10 seconds.
Place both thumbs side-by-side on the lower third/centre of the breastbone encircling the chest with your hands (or use two fingers perpendicular to the breastbone).
Give 30 chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute, pressing at least one-third of the chest depth (approximately 4 cm / 1.5 inches) and allowing full chest recoil.
Cover BOTH the baby's mouth and nose with your mouth and give 2 steady rescue breaths (1 second each) until the chest or abdomen visibly rises.
Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths (or 15:2 if specifically trained) until EMS arrives or the baby cries, moves purposefully, and breathes normally.

conditionalActions.condition: If you are alone and have NO phone nearby
conditionalActions.action: Perform 1 minute of CPR before pausing briefly to access 911.

conditionalActions.condition: If you are unable or unwilling to give rescue breaths
conditionalActions.action: Perform continuous chest compressions at 100–120 per minute without stopping.

conditionalActions.condition: If an AED is available
conditionalActions.action: Prefer a paediatric AED or paediatric pads placed front-and-back (anterior-posterior) so pads do not overlap; use adult pads if paediatric pads are unavailable.

warnings: Do NOT tilt a baby's head far backward—over-extension narrows an infant's soft airway; keep the head in a neutral position.
Do NOT shake a baby to check responsiveness—tap the sole of the foot instead.
Blow gently—only enough air to see the baby's chest rise over 1 second.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for any unresponsive infant with absent or abnormal breathing

learnMore.overview: Cardiac arrest in babies under 1 year almost always stems from airway obstruction or breathing failure. The two-thumb chest-encircling technique (especially preferred in newborns) delivers consistent compression depth (~4 cm) with less rescuer fatigue, paired with gentle mouth-to-mouth-and-nose rescue breaths.
causes: Choking on milk/food or small objects, drowning, severe bronchiolitis/respiratory infection, or birth asphyxia
riskFactors: Unsafe sleep environments, small household objects within reach, or unsupervised bathing
detailedRecognition: Applies to infants under approximately 1 year of age.
An unresponsive infant feels floppy/limp, makes no cry or purposeful movement on foot tap, and may look pale or bluish.
prevention: Follow safe infant sleep practices (back to sleep on a firm, clear surface), keep small objects and button batteries locked away, and never leave a baby unattended in water.
preparation: Parents and caregivers of newborns and infants are strongly encouraged to practise infant CPR and choking relief.
explanations: An infant's tongue is relatively large and trachea pliable, so a neutral head tilt opens the airway best without kinking it.
Two-thumb encircling compressions over the lower third of the sternum generate higher blood pressure and better depth consistency than two-finger compressions, though both are effective.
additionalPrecautions: Rotate compressors every 1 to 2 minutes if a second rescuer is available.
followUpCare: Monitor breathing continuously until EMS assumes care, even if the baby begins crying and breathing normally.

source.topicTitle: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Continue chest compressions while turning on the AED, attach the pads to bare dry skin, and follow the voice prompts.
recognitionSigns: Person is unresponsive and not breathing normally (or only gasping)
An Automated External Defibrillator (AED) has arrived at the scene during CPR
steps: Keep CPR going while a second person opens and turns on the AED (if alone, switch it on immediately and follow voice prompts).
Expose and dry the chest; apply the self-adhesive pads firmly to bare skin as shown on the pad diagrams (upper right chest below collarbone and left side below armpit).
Stop touching the person as soon as the AED announces rhythm analysis, and tell everyone nearby, 'Stand clear!'
Deliver the shock if advised: verify no one is touching the person, shout a clear warning, and press the flashing shock button (fully automatic AEDs shock automatically).
Resume chest compressions immediately after the shock (or immediately if 'no shock advised') without pausing to check pulse or breathing.
Leave the pads attached and follow the AED's 2-minute prompts until EMS takes over or the person wakes and breathes normally.

conditionalActions.condition: If the patient is a baby or child under 8 years old
conditionalActions.action: Use (1) a paediatric AED or paediatric pads first; if unavailable, use a standard AED with adult pads, placing one pad on the front chest and one on the back (anterior-posterior) if needed so pads stay 1–2 cm apart without overlapping.

conditionalActions.condition: If the chest is wet (sweat or drowning) or very hairy
conditionalActions.action: Wipe the chest dry before sticking pads; shave/remove excessive hair only if it can be done with minimal delay.

conditionalActions.condition: If applying pads to a large-breasted person
conditionalActions.action: Place the left pad beside or underneath the left breast avoiding breast tissue; adjust rather than waste time removing a bra if bare skin is accessible.

warnings: Never touch the casualty while the AED is analysing the heart rhythm or delivering a shock.
Never peel pads off to swap them if you placed them in reversed positions—leave them on so adhesion and time are not lost.
Do not use an AED in standing water, and turn off/remove any high-flow oxygen blowing across the chest before shocking.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately in all cardiac arrest events and inform dispatchers that an AED is in use

learnMore.overview: An Automated External Defibrillator (AED) safely analyses the heart's electrical rhythm and delivers a life-saving shock only when a shockable rhythm (such as ventricular fibrillation) is present. Any layperson can use a public-access AED safely by following its voice and visual prompts.
causes: Sudden cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia
riskFactors: Every minute of delay before defibrillation sharply lowers survival; locked cabinets or hesitation delay shock delivery
detailedRecognition: An AED will NEVER shock a normal beating heart; it only advises or delivers a shock when a life-threatening shockable rhythm is detected.
prevention: Note the locations and green/white signage of public-access AEDs in schools, malls, airports, gyms, and offices.
preparation: Practise seamless teamwork: one responder compresses the chest while another attaches the AED pads to keep hands-off pauses under 10 seconds.
explanations: CPR alone rarely restarts a fibrillating heart—it buys time until the AED shock resets the heart's electrical system.
Immediate chest compressions right after a shock (without pausing for a pulse/rhythm check) significantly improve survival.
additionalPrecautions: Ensure electrode pads never touch or overlap; maintain at least a 1–2 cm gap between pads.
followUpCare: Keep AED pads attached and monitor breathing closely even after recovery, as abnormal heart rhythms can recur before EMS arrives.

source.topicTitle: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing when a defibrillator is available

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Start CPR immediately (with rescue breaths if able), call 911, and administer naloxone if available without delaying CPR.
recognitionSigns: Unresponsive or extremely drowsy after known or suspected opioid use (pills, patches, syringes, or blister packs nearby)
Very slow, shallow, snoring, gurgling, or absent breathing
steps: Check scene safety (watch for uncapped needles) and check responsiveness and normal breathing for up to 10 seconds.
Shout for help and call 911 immediately (on speakerphone if alone), asking bystanders to bring naloxone and an AED.
Begin CPR immediately (30 compressions : 2 rescue breaths if able and willing, or continuous chest compressions) if breathing is absent or abnormal.
Administer naloxone (nasal spray or outer-thigh/upper-arm intramuscular injection per package instructions) as soon as available and legally permitted, pausing CPR only if strictly necessary.
Continue CPR until the person breathes normally and shows signs of life or EMS takes over.
Give a second dose of naloxone if there is no improvement after 5 minutes or if overdose breathing problems return.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person wakes up and breathes normally
conditionalActions.action: Place them on their side if still drowsy, step back slightly in case they wake confused or agitated, and monitor breathing closely until EMS arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If you are alone and naloxone is visible nearby
conditionalActions.action: Quickly retrieve it, call 911 on speakerphone, start CPR, and administer naloxone.

warnings: Never delay starting CPR to search for naloxone or read instructions—high-quality CPR is the primary life-saving action in cardiac arrest.
Always keep EMS coming even if the person wakes after naloxone—naloxone wears off (often within minutes) and fatal respiratory arrest can return.
Be prepared for sudden confusion or agitation when naloxone reverses opioid effects.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for every suspected opioid overdose, even if naloxone restores breathing

learnMore.overview: Opioids depress the brain's drive to breathe, causing slow or stopped breathing followed by cardiac arrest. Timely airway support, CPR with rescue breaths, and the antidote naloxone can reverse fatal respiratory depression.
causes: Excessive dose of prescription opioids, illicit opioids, or opioids combined with alcohol or sedatives
riskFactors: Mixing opioids with alcohol or benzodiazepines, resumed use after reduced tolerance, or high-potency synthetic opioids
detailedRecognition: Snoring or gurgling sounds in an unarousable person are classic signs of life-threatening airway/breathing depression, not deep sleep.
Note that a person with opioid toxicity may still react slightly to painful stimuli on the AVPU scale while having dangerously slow breathing.
prevention: Take prescription opioids strictly as directed, never mix with alcohol, and lock medications away from children.
Carry naloxone and learn how to use it if caring for someone at risk of opioid overdose.
preparation: Record the time and number of naloxone doses given to report to EMS.
explanations: Because opioid cardiac arrest stems from oxygen deprivation (hypoxia), rescue breaths alongside chest compressions are strongly encouraged when the responder is willing.
Naloxone works only on opioids and has a shorter duration than many long-acting opioids, making medical observation essential.
additionalPrecautions: Treat affected individuals with dignity and non-judgmental care.
followUpCare: Ensure hospital transport and prolonged observation for recurrent respiratory depression.

source.topicTitle: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with suspected opioid overdose

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stay out of the water—reach with a pole/branch or throw something that floats, call 911, and start CPR with rescue breaths once on land if not breathing normally.
recognitionSigns: Vertical body position ('climbing an invisible ladder'), mouth at/below water level, bobbing with no forward progress, or silent submersion
Unresponsive, gasping, coughing, or not breathing after removal from water
steps: Shout for a lifeguard/bystanders and call 911 while keeping your eyes fixed on the person's location in the water.
Rescue without entering the water: reach from shore/boat with a rigid object (pole, branch, towel) or throw flotation (ring buoy, lifejacket, sealed container, rope).
Remove the person onto land or a stable boat as quickly as possible (do not delay removal of an unresponsive person for spinal concerns).
Check responsiveness and normal breathing for up to 10 seconds immediately once out of the water.
Open the airway and give 2 to 5 steady rescue breaths (1 second each for visible chest rise), then continue 30:2 CPR with rescue breaths if unresponsive with absent or abnormal breathing.
Dry the chest before attaching AED pads if an AED is available, and roll the person onto their side briefly only if vomit blocks the airway.
Remove wet clothes, cover with dry blankets insulated from cold ground, and monitor closely until EMS arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is unresponsive but breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Place them in the recovery position on their side so fluids can drain freely, keep them warm, and call 911.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is responsive and breathing after rescue
conditionalActions.action: Help them sit or lie comfortably, keep them warm, seek medical evaluation if coughing heavily or short of breath, and ensure someone monitors them for around 8 hours.

conditionalActions.condition: If you are unable or unwilling to give rescue breaths during CPR
conditionalActions.action: Perform continuous chest compressions at 100–120 per minute without delay.

warnings: Do NOT swim out to touch an actively drowning person without training and a flotation barrier—panicking victims frequently pull rescuers underwater.
Do NOT attempt in-water resuscitation unless specifically and repeatedly trained in aquatic contact rescue.
NEVER perform abdominal thrusts, hang a person upside down, or try to 'drain water' from the lungs—this delays CPR and causes vomiting/injury.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for any drowning rescue, loss of consciousness, CPR, persistent coughing, or breathing difficulty (which can worsen over 8 hours)

learnMore.overview: Drowning is often silent and rapid—victims rarely wave or shout because all effort goes into trying to breathe. Safe non-contact flotation rescue followed by immediate airway opening and rescue breaths with CPR reverses life-threatening oxygen deprivation.
causes: Submersion in open water, floods, pools, rivers, ditches, or household bathtubs/buckets
riskFactors: Unsupervised children under 5 years, alcohol use near water, lack of lifejackets, rip currents, or underlying epilepsy/cardiac conditions
detailedRecognition: Early distress signs include head tilted back with mouth at water level, hair over forehead/eyes, hyperventilating/gasping, vertical posture without leg kick, or sudden disappearance.
prevention: Install four-sided barriers around pools/water hazards, enforce constant close adult supervision of children, wear lifejackets on boats, and swim with a buddy.
preparation: Keep throw ropes, ring buoys, or flotation aids accessible near bodies of water and anchor the end of any lifeline before throwing.
explanations: Aspirated water is absorbed quickly and does not block the trachea like a solid object; rescue breaths deliver urgently needed oxygen to stop hypoxic brain and heart injury.
Delayed lung complications can develop hours after rescue, requiring observation for ~8 hours and medical assessment for any cough or breathlessness.
additionalPrecautions: Watch for hypothermia in anyone rescued from water, even in mild weather.
followUpCare: Ensure hospital evaluation for anyone who required rescue breaths, CPR, lost consciousness, or develops coughing, foam, fever, or shortness of breath.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Help the person sit upright or lean forward bracing their arms on a support, loosen tight clothing, and call 911 if severe.
recognitionSigns: Shortness of breath, chest tightness, noisy/laboured breathing, or inability to count to 10 in one breath
Using neck/shoulder muscles to breathe, flaring nostrils, or bluish lips, ears, or fingertips
Abnormally fast breathing (>20/min adult, >30 child, >40 baby) or dangerously slow breathing (<10/min adult, <15 child, <25 baby)
steps: Check the scene first for smoke, fumes, or carbon monoxide hazards before staying in the room.
Help the person into a comfortable seated position—leaning slightly forward with arms braced on knees or a table often eases breathing.
Loosen any tight clothing around the neck, chest, or waist and reassure them calmly.
Assist the person in taking their own prescribed breathing medication (such as an inhaler) if they have it.
Call 911 immediately if breathing is severe, lips/fingers turn bluish, breathing slows down, chest pain or confusion/drowsiness occurs, or medication does not help within a few minutes.
Stay with the person, keep the environment calm, and monitor responsiveness and breathing until recovery or EMS arrival.

conditionalActions.condition: If hyperventilation from panic/anxiety is suspected (rapid breathing with tingling hands/mouth and dizziness)
conditionalActions.action: Move to a quiet space, reassure calmly, and guide slow steady breaths (inhale 1 count through nose, exhale 3 counts through mouth); call 911 if it continues or a medical cause is possible.

conditionalActions.condition: If breathing does not improve after 10–15 minutes even when mild
conditionalActions.action: Seek prompt medical care.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive
conditionalActions.action: Open the airway, check breathing, and start CPR immediately if breathing is absent or abnormal (consider naloxone if opioid toxicity is suspected).

warnings: Do NOT have a hyperventilating person breathe into a paper bag—serious medical emergencies like asthma, heart attack, or hypoxia can look like hyperventilation.
Do NOT force someone struggling to breathe to lie flat on their back.
Watch closely for slowing breathing or drowsiness—these signal life-threatening exhaustion.
emergencyEscalation: Severe shortness of breath, acute chest pain, or bluish skin on lips, ears, or fingers
Confusion, drowsiness, or unresponsiveness
Abnormally slow breathing or prescribed inhaler failing to relieve symptoms within a few minutes
No improvement after 10–15 minutes

learnMore.overview: Breathing difficulties range from anxiety-related hyperventilation to life-threatening emergencies such as choking, severe asthma, COPD flare-ups, anaphylaxis, pneumonia, croup, heart failure, or toxic gas inhalation.
causes: Asthma, COPD, respiratory infections (pneumonia, bronchiolitis, croup), choking, anaphylaxis, heart attack/heart failure, carbon monoxide/smoke inhalation, or acute anxiety
riskFactors: Chronic lung or heart conditions, heavy air pollution/wildfire smoke, allergens, confined combustion spaces, or young/elderly age
detailedRecognition: Normal adult breathing is 10–20 breaths/min; >20 (adult), >30 (child), >40 (baby) is rapid, while <10 (adult), <15 (child), <25 (baby) is dangerously slow.
Hyperventilation often causes lightheadedness, sweating, and tingling around the fingers, feet, or mouth.
prevention: Avoid entering smoky or poorly ventilated fuel-burning areas, limit strenuous outdoor exertion during heavy pollution/smog, and keep prescribed reliever inhalers accessible.
preparation: Know if family members, classmates, or coworkers have asthma, severe allergies, or heart/lung conditions.
explanations: Sitting upright or bracing the arms forward (tripod posture) reduces pressure on the diaphragm and helps accessory chest muscles expand the lungs.
Slow, coached nasal-in / mouth-out breathing helps restore calm during hyperventilation without risking hypoxia.
additionalPrecautions: Supplementary oxygen should only be administered by specifically trained providers when available and indicated.
followUpCare: Advise medical evaluation for any first-time or recurring episodes of unexplained shortness of breath.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Ask 'Are you choking?'—if they cannot cough, speak, or breathe, give up to 5 firm back blows followed by up to 5 abdominal thrusts.
recognitionSigns: Complete blockage: Unable to speak, cough, or breathe; clutching the throat; silent panic or bluish lips
Partial blockage: Can still speak, breathe, or cough forcefully (may wheeze between coughs)
steps: Ask, 'Are you choking?' If they can cough forcefully or speak, encourage them to keep coughing and do NOT slap their back.
Act immediately if they cannot cough, speak, or breathe: lean the person forward and give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.
Stand behind them if back blows fail, place a fist between their ribs and belly button, grasp it with your other hand, and pull sharply inward and upward up to 5 times (abdominal thrusts).
Call 911 immediately (or have a bystander call) if the blockage does not clear, and keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts.
Lower the person to a firm floor and start standard CPR (30 compressions : 2 rescue breaths) immediately if they become unresponsive.

conditionalActions.condition: If the choking adult is visibly pregnant or you cannot wrap your arms around their abdomen
conditionalActions.action: Use firm chest thrusts on the centre of the breastbone instead of abdominal thrusts, alternating with 5 back blows.

conditionalActions.condition: If a solid object becomes clearly visible in the mouth
conditionalActions.action: Carefully remove it with your fingers ONLY if you can clearly see it.

warnings: NEVER perform a blind finger sweep inside the mouth—it can push the object deeper into the airway.
Do NOT slap or thrust someone with a partial obstruction who is coughing effectively—their own cough clears the airway best.
Do not rely on commercial suction airway-clearance devices instead of immediate back blows and thrusts.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately if complete airway obstruction is not cleared promptly or the person becomes unresponsive
Always seek medical evaluation after abdominal thrusts or complete choking, even after the object comes out (risk of internal injury or residual fragments)

learnMore.overview: Foreign-body airway obstruction (choking) cuts off oxygen within minutes. Stepwise care—encouraging coughing for partial blockages, starting with 5 firm back blows for complete blockages, and escalating to 5 abdominal thrusts—maximizes relief while minimizing internal injury.
causes: Food pieces eaten quickly or while talking/laughing, poorly chewed meat, or dental prostheses
riskFactors: Older age, alcohol intoxication, poor dentition, stroke, Parkinson's disease, or swallowing disorders
detailedRecognition: Differentiate complete obstruction (silent inability to cough/speak/breathe) from partial obstruction (coughing/speaking) and from asthma or anaphylaxis.
prevention: Cut food into manageable pieces, chew slowly, avoid talking or laughing with a full mouth, and supervise high-risk older adults during meals.
preparation: Remember that a gentle pat will not dislodge a wedged object—back blows and thrusts must be firm and decisive.
explanations: Large bystander cohort data (ILCOR 2025 update) show initial back blows achieve higher obstruction relief and survival with fewer complications than starting with abdominal thrusts.
Abdominal thrusts compress air remaining in the lungs to expel the blockage when back blows alone do not succeed.
additionalPrecautions: Never give water or food to 'wash down' an airway obstruction.
followUpCare: Ensure medical assessment after any abdominal/chest thrusts or if persistent coughing or swallowing pain remains.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: If a child (1 year or older) cannot cough, cry, or breathe, lean them forward and give up to 5 firm back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts.
recognitionSigns: Complete blockage: Sudden inability to cough, speak, cry, or breathe; silent gagging, panic, or bluish lips
Partial blockage: Child is crying, speaking, or coughing forcefully
steps: Encourage the child to cough if they can cough, cry, or speak—stay with them and monitor closely without slapping their back.
Act at once if the child cannot cough, cry, or breathe: kneel or bend to the child's height, lean them forward, and give up to 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades.
Kneel behind the child if back blows fail, place your fist between their ribs and belly button, and pull sharply inward and upward up to 5 times (adapting force to the child's size).
Call 911 immediately if the object does not clear, and continue alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts.
Place the child on a firm surface and start Child CPR (30 compressions : 2 rescue breaths) immediately if they become unresponsive.

conditionalActions.condition: If the child is under 1 year old (infant/baby)
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT use abdominal thrusts—switch immediately to Infant Choking (5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts).

conditionalActions.condition: If a foreign object is clearly visible in the child's mouth
conditionalActions.action: Remove it carefully with your fingers ONLY if you can see it clearly.

warnings: NEVER perform a blind finger sweep in a child's mouth—it can push a coin, grape, or toy deeper and seal the airway.
Do NOT give a choking child water to drink or hold them upside down.
Always get medical evaluation after abdominal thrusts or complete choking.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for complete airway obstruction or unresponsiveness
Urgent medical evaluation after abdominal thrusts, suspected button battery/magnet ingestion, or persistent coughing/swallowing difficulty

learnMore.overview: Children aged 1 year and older explore with food and small objects and can choke while running or playing. Prompt back blows followed by size-adapted abdominal thrusts clear most complete airway blockages.
causes: Round or hard foods (whole grapes, nuts, hard candy, hotdog rounds) and small items (coins, marbles, small toy parts, button batteries)
riskFactors: Running or laughing with food in the mouth, young children under 5 years, or access to small household items
detailedRecognition: Applies to children aged 1 year and older; babies under 1 year require chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.
Distinguish sudden silent choking from croup or asthma (which develop with coughing/wheezing and illness signs).
prevention: Cut round foods lengthwise into small pieces, have children sit while eating, and keep coins, magnets, and small toys out of reach of young children.
preparation: Kneeling behind a child aligns your arms properly and helps control thrust force appropriate to their body size.
explanations: Leaning the child forward uses gravity alongside the vibration of back blows to expel the foreign object.
Starting CPR if the child becomes unresponsive generates airway pressure that can also dislodge the obstruction.
additionalPrecautions: If a button battery or magnet was swallowed rather than inhaled, treat immediately under Poisoning—button batteries burn the oesophagus rapidly.
followUpCare: Have a doctor check any child who received abdominal thrusts or had a complete choking episode.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Support the baby face-down on your forearm/lap with head lower than body and give up to 5 firm back blows, then turn face-up for up to 5 chest thrusts—NEVER abdominal thrusts.
recognitionSigns: Complete blockage: Baby (under 1 year) suddenly cannot cry, cough, or breathe; silent open mouth or bluish lips/face
Partial blockage: Baby is crying out or coughing
steps: Wait and watch closely if the baby is coughing or crying—let them cough to clear their own airway without interfering.
Sit or kneel if the baby cannot cough, cry, or breathe, lay the baby face-down along your forearm/lap supporting the head and jaw with your hand, keeping the head lower than the body.
Give up to 5 firm back blows between the baby's shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

Turn the baby face-up onto your knees/forearm supporting the head and neck if back blows fail, and give up to 5 sharp chest thrusts on the lower breastbone (using two-thumb encircling hands or two fingers).
Call 911 immediately if the object is not cleared, and continue alternating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts.
Place the baby on a firm flat surface and start Infant CPR (30 compressions : 2 mouth-to-mouth-and-nose breaths) immediately if the baby becomes limp/unresponsive.

conditionalActions.condition: If solid material becomes clearly visible in the baby's mouth
conditionalActions.action: Pick it out carefully with your fingers ONLY if you can see it clearly.

warnings: NEVER perform abdominal thrusts on an infant under 1 year old—their developing abdominal organs (especially the liver) can be severely injured.
NEVER do a blind finger sweep in a baby's mouth and NEVER hold or shake a baby upside down by the legs.
Support the baby across your lap while seated or kneeling rather than unsupported on one arm so you do not drop them.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately if complete obstruction does not clear after the first cycle or if the baby becomes unresponsive
Always seek medical evaluation after any complete choking episode or chest thrusts in an infant

learnMore.overview: Babies under 1 year frequently put objects in their mouths and are learning to swallow solids. Because abdominal thrusts can damage fragile infant organs, infants with complete choking receive alternating cycles of 5 supported face-down back blows and 5 sharp chest thrusts.
causes: Milk/food chunks during weaning, small toys, coins, buttons, latex balloon pieces, or button batteries
riskFactors: Older siblings' small toys within reach, propping feeding bottles, or inappropriate solid food textures
detailedRecognition: Gagging/coughing noisy reflexes while learning solids are common partial events—only intervene physically if the cough becomes silent/ineffective and the baby cannot cry or breathe.
prevention: Keep all small items (smaller than a toilet-paper roll opening), coins, and button batteries completely out of reach, and supervise every feeding.
preparation: Sitting or kneeling to rest your forearm on your thigh/lap gives far safer support for a real infant's weight and length than standing.
explanations: Holding the head lower than the chest lets gravity assist the pressure wave created by back blows and sharp chest thrusts.
Two-thumb encircling or two-finger chest thrusts safely compress the infant ribcage without crushing abdominal organs.
additionalPrecautions: Never slap the baby's head or press on the soft tip of the breastbone/stomach.
followUpCare: Have a doctor examine the infant after any complete airway obstruction to check for airway irritation or aspirated fragments.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Help the person sit upright in a comfortable position, reassure them, and assist them in using their prescribed reliever inhaler.
recognitionSigns: Difficulty breathing with wheezing (whistling sound), coughing, and chest tightness
Difficulty speaking full sentences, rapid breathing, or sitting hunched forward
Severe danger signs: Bluish lips/fingers, drowsiness/confusion, or breathing becoming slow, quiet, and exhausted
steps: Help the person sit upright or lean slightly forward bracing their arms on a support, and reassure them calmly.
Move them away from obvious triggers (such as smoke, dust, or fumes) and loosen any tight clothing.
Assist the person in using their prescribed bronchodilator (reliever) inhaler, fitting a spacer device if available (especially for children).
Call 911 immediately if they have no inhaler and the attack lasts several minutes, the inhaler does not help within a few minutes, or severe danger signs appear.
Stay with the person, keep them calm, and support additional doses of their prescribed inhaler per their asthma action plan/label while waiting for EMS.

conditionalActions.condition: If no inhaler is available
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 if the attack persists beyond a few minutes or is severe, seat them upright near fresh clean air, loosen tight clothing, and keep them calm.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 and start CPR immediately.

warnings: Do NOT mistake quieter wheezing and slower breathing in an exhausted person for improvement—a 'silent chest' is a life-threatening emergency.
Do NOT force someone having an asthma attack to lie down flat.
Use only the person's prescribed reliever inhaler (not a daily steroid preventer inhaler unless specified as combination reliever).
emergencyEscalation: No inhaler available and symptoms last several minutes
Inhaler brings no relief within a few minutes
Severe difficulty breathing, inability to speak, or exhaustion
Bluish colour on lips, ears, fingers, or toes
Confusion, drowsiness, or slow/quiet breathing

learnMore.overview: During an asthma attack, the airways in the lungs swell, narrow, and produce extra mucus, making it hard to move air out and in. Prompt upright positioning, calm reassurance, and prescribed bronchodilator inhaler use can rapidly reopen airways and prevent fatal respiratory arrest.
causes: Respiratory viral infections, smoke, dust mites, pollen, animal dander, cold air, air pollution, exercise, or strong stress
riskFactors: History of asthma or allergies, missed preventive medication, or lack of an accessible reliever inhaler
detailedRecognition: People with asthma often recognize an attack starting and carry a quick-relief bronchodilator inhaler.
Anxiety during breathlessness can worsen airway tightness, making calm reassurance important.
prevention: Take prescribed controller/preventive medication regularly, carry a reliever inhaler and spacer, and avoid known triggers like tobacco smoke.
preparation: Schools, families, and workplaces should know students' or coworkers' asthma action plans and keep spacers clean and accessible.
explanations: Bronchodilator inhalers relax tightened airway muscles within minutes.
Attaching a spacer to a metered-dose inhaler delivers more medication into the lungs rather than the back of the throat, especially in children.
additionalPrecautions: Mild tremor or faster heartbeat can occur after bronchodilator puffs; continue monitoring breathing and alertness.
followUpCare: Advise medical review after any severe attack or if reliever inhaler use increases.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Calmly reassure the child and help them sit upright in a comfortable position that makes breathing easiest.
recognitionSigns: Child (usually 6 years or younger) with a distinctive hoarse, 'barking' cough and croaky voice
Raspy, squeaky, or high-pitched sound when breathing in (stridor), often worse at night or when crying
steps: Stay calm, comfort the child, and hold or seat them upright—crying and distress make upper-airway swelling worse.
Check the child's temperature and treat any fever appropriately.
Allow the child to breathe warm, humidified air if it can be done safely without any burn risk (for example, sitting with a caregiver in a bathroom near a warm running shower).
Watch their breathing and alertness closely—symptoms can worsen from mild to severe within a few hours.
Call 911 immediately if the child has severe difficulty breathing, chest/neck skin pulling inward, nostril flaring, drooling, or does not improve.

conditionalActions.condition: If the child sits bent forward with an open mouth, drooling, high fever, and no barking cough (suspected epiglottitis)
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT examine inside the throat or lay them flat—keep them calm upright and call 911 immediately.

warnings: NEVER place a child over boiling/scalding water or in a hot bath where steam or spills can cause severe burns.
Do NOT put fingers or objects inside the child's throat.
If in any doubt between croup, choking, or epiglottitis, call 911 immediately.
emergencyEscalation: Severe shortness of breath or stridor even when resting calmly
Hollow/sucking-in at the base of the neck or ribs, flaring nostrils, or leaning forward with open mouth
Drooling, inability to swallow, bluish lips, drowsiness, or persistent/worsening symptoms

learnMore.overview: Croup is a viral inflammation of the upper airway (larynx and windpipe), most common in children aged 6 years and under. Swelling narrows the airway, causing a barking cough, hoarse cry/voice, and squeaky inspiratory stridor.
causes: Viral upper-respiratory infections (such as parainfluenza viruses) causing swelling around the vocal cords
riskFactors: Children aged 6 months to 6 years; symptoms characteristically flare at night
detailedRecognition: Remember CRY: Cough/cry in a hoarse barking voice, Respiratory distress, Young child.
Epiglottitis is a rarer, life-threatening bacterial swelling of the throat flap presenting with sudden fever, muffled voice, drooling, and severe distress without a barking cough.
prevention: Practise hand hygiene and keep childhood immunizations (including Haemophilus influenzae type b against epiglottitis) up to date.
preparation: Parents of young children should know how to recognize chest/neck retractions and stridor at rest.
explanations: Keeping the child calm and seated upright reduces turbulent airflow through the narrowed upper airway.
While evidence for humidified air is limited, safe warm bathroom humidity can soothe and distract an anxious child when scald hazards are avoided.
additionalPrecautions: Do not give hot drinks to young children with croup (no evidence of benefit and high scald risk).
followUpCare: Seek medical evaluation if croup symptoms persist, recur, or interfere with drinking fluids.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Apply firm, continuous direct pressure directly over the bleeding wound immediately and call 911.
recognitionSigns: Blood flowing heavily, gushing, or spurting from a wound
Blood rapidly soaking through clothing/bandages or pooling on the ground
Pale, cold, clammy skin, dizziness, or weakness (signs of shock)
steps: Protect your hands with gloves or a clean barrier (or ask the injured person to press firmly on their own wound right away).
Press firmly and continuously directly over the source of bleeding using clean gauze, a folded towel, or clean clothing.
Help the person lie down and call 911 immediately (use speakerphone if alone).
Add a second dressing directly on top and press harder if blood soaks through the first dressing.

Apply a manufactured tourniquet (5–7 cm / 2–3 inches above the wound, never over a joint) or pack a haemostatic dressing with direct pressure ONLY if severe bleeding is on an arm or leg and direct pressure fails or cannot be maintained.
Keep the person warm with a blanket or coat to help prevent shock, and monitor breathing and responsiveness until EMS arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If an object (such as glass, metal, or a knife) is embedded in the wound
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT remove it—apply firm pressure around the edges of the object to control bleeding and stabilize it in place.

conditionalActions.condition: If a limb tourniquet is applied and bleeding still continues
conditionalActions.action: Tighten the tourniquet further; if still bleeding, apply a second tourniquet above the first and never loosen or remove a tourniquet once applied.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Ensure major bleeding is compressed/tourniqueted and start CPR immediately.

warnings: Do NOT use indirect 'pressure points' or ice to try to stop severe bleeding.
NEVER remove an impaled or embedded object—it may be plugging major blood vessels.
NEVER apply a tourniquet to the head, neck, chest, or abdomen, and never loosen an applied limb tourniquet before medical professionals take over.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for all severe or uncontrolled external bleeding, tourniquet application, embedded objects, or signs of shock

learnMore.overview: Uncontrolled external haemorrhage is the leading preventable cause of death in trauma. Immediate, forceful direct manual pressure stops most bleeds, while manufactured windlass tourniquets and haemostatic dressings save lives in severe limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot control.
causes: Road traffic collisions, machinery or tool accidents, deep glass lacerations, gunshot or stab wounds, or blast injuries
riskFactors: Anticoagulant (blood-thinning) medications, clotting disorders, or delayed pressure application
detailedRecognition: Even about 180 mL (a cupful) of rapid blood loss can start dangerous deterioration if not stopped early; thick clothing or soil can hide pooled blood.
prevention: Use machine guards, protective workwear, and road safety equipment, and include trauma dressings and gloves in workplace/vehicle kits.
preparation: Pressing with two straight locked arms delivers far more sustained force than pressing with bent elbows.
explanations: Direct manual pressure compresses severed vessels so blood can clot; stacking too many loose bandages dilutes force unless firm pressure is maintained.

Manufactured windlass tourniquets reliably stop arterial limb flow in adults and children aged 2–16 years, whereas improvised tourniquets have high failure rates and should only be used as a last resort.
additionalPrecautions: Warn a conscious casualty that a properly tightened tourniquet is very painful so they do not try to loosen it, and note the time applied for EMS.
followUpCare: Urgent hospital surgical/wound care and shock monitoring are required for all severe bleeds.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 immediately, help the person rest in a comfortable position, control external bleeding carefully without sealing an open chest wound, and never push protruding organs back in.
recognitionSigns: Penetrating wound or severe blow to the chest or abdomen
Chest injury: Painful/difficult breathing, coughing blood, or a bubbling/sucking sound at a chest wound
Abdominal injury: Severe belly pain, external bleeding, protruding tissue/organs, or signs of shock
steps: Ensure the scene is safe (especially after violence or road crashes) and call 911 immediately.
Position comfortably: for a chest injury, help them sit semi-propped leaning slightly toward the injured side; for an abdominal injury, help them lie on their back with knees bent.
Control active bleeding with direct hand pressure—for an open chest wound, ensure your pressure or any dressing does NOT completely seal the wound.
Leave a non-bleeding open chest wound uncovered (or use only a non-occlusive dressing during long transport, checking constantly that clotting blood does not seal it).
Cover any open abdominal wound with protruding organs loosely using a sterile or clean WET dressing without pressing on or pushing organs back inside.
Keep the person warm and monitor breathing, alertness, and signs of shock closely until EMS arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If an object is impaled in the chest or abdomen
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT remove it—stabilize it gently in place (loosely if pulsating) and control bleeding around it.

conditionalActions.condition: If a dressing on an open chest wound becomes soaked/clotted and breathing worsens
conditionalActions.action: Loosen or remove the dressing immediately so trapped air can escape.

warnings: NEVER apply an airtight (occlusive) dressing to an open chest wound—trapped air can collapse the lung and cause fatal tension pneumothorax.
NEVER push protruding abdominal organs back into the body or give food or water.
Never remove an impaled object.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for all penetrating chest or abdominal wounds, suspected internal bleeding, coughing blood, breathing distress, or shock

learnMore.overview: Chest and abdominal trauma can injure the heart, lungs, major blood vessels, or abdominal organs, causing rapid internal bleeding or collapsed lung. Careful positioning, non-occlusive open-chest care, and moist protection of abdominal wounds prevent life-threatening complications while EMS responds.
causes: Road traffic crashes, falls from height, crush injuries, stab or gunshot wounds, or industrial impacts
riskFactors: High-speed collisions, lack of seatbelts, or hazardous construction/conflict environments
detailedRecognition: Internal chest or abdominal bleeding may show no external wound at first—watch closely for pale clammy skin, fast pulse/breathing, dizziness, and thirst (shock).
A single projectile or impact can cause multiple entry/exit wounds hidden under clothing.
prevention: Wear seatbelts and workplace protective gear, and never approach an active violence scene until secured.
preparation: Understand the difference between an occlusive seal (avoided in lay first aid) and leaving an open chest wound able to vent air.
explanations: ILCOR recommends against lay providers applying occlusive dressings to open chest wounds because blood clots can turn any seal into a one-way valve that builds lethal chest pressure.
Bending the knees in abdominal trauma relaxes abdominal wall tension and pain.
additionalPrecautions: Do not give anything to eat or drink, as urgent surgery is often required.
followUpCare: Immediate hospital trauma evaluation is mandatory even if external wounds appear small.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Control life-threatening bleeding first with firm direct pressure (or a limb tourniquet if needed), call 911, and keep the severed part dry and cool.
recognitionSigns: Complete amputation: A finger, toe, hand, arm, or leg is completely severed from the body
Partial amputation: Part of a limb is nearly severed but remains partially attached
steps: Call 911 immediately and stop heavy bleeding on the injured stump using firm direct pressure (apply a tourniquet above a severe limb bleed if direct pressure fails).
Help the person lie down, cover the wound with a sterile dressing or clean cloth, and keep them warm to treat for shock.
Retrieve the completely severed body part once bleeding is controlled, wrap it gently in sterile gauze or a clean dry cloth, and seal it inside a clean watertight plastic bag.
Place that sealed bag inside a second bag or container of ice and cold water so it stays cool without ever touching water or ice directly.
