Support and immobilize a partially amputated limb in normal alignment using clean dressings (do NOT straighten an angulated fracture).
Send the cooled, labelled severed part to the hospital with the injured person, and offer calm emotional support.

conditionalActions.condition: If hospital arrival is within a few hours
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT give food or drink because emergency surgery and anaesthesia will likely be needed.

conditionalActions.condition: If minor oozing continues from the bone marrow after applying a tourniquet
conditionalActions.action: Keep the tourniquet securely tightened in place (stop-gushing control indicates it is working) and maintain direct dressing pressure.

warnings: NEVER place a severed body part directly into water or directly onto ice—waterlogging and freezing destroy tissue and prevent surgical reattachment.
Never prioritize searching for a severed part over stopping life-threatening bleeding on the person.
Never cut skin bridges on a partial amputation.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for every complete or partial amputation and alert EMS so surgical replantation care can prepare

learnMore.overview: Amputations are dramatic, psychologically distressing injuries that can cause rapid blood loss, yet severed fingers, hands, and limbs can sometimes be surgically reattached when bleeding is controlled first and the amputated part is preserved dry and cool.
causes: Power tools, industrial or kitchen machinery, road traffic crashes, fireworks, or blast injuries
riskFactors: Operating unguarded saws/machinery, handling fireworks, or high-speed motorcycle/vehicle collisions
detailedRecognition: Distinguish complete separation (requires dry bag-in-ice-water preservation) from partial attachment (requires gentle support and splinting in place).
prevention: Use automatic shut-off guards on machinery, wear protective equipment, and never handle illegal or unlit fireworks.
preparation: Wear gloves or clean hand barriers—amputations are major open wounds with bloodborne exposure risks.
explanations: Indirect cooling (sealed dry bag placed in ice-water bath) slows tissue death without causing frostbite damage to cells.
Injured persons and witnesses often experience intense emotional shock, making calm Psychological First Aid vital.
additionalPrecautions: Immobilize the injured limb during transport to prevent further vessel or nerve tearing.
followUpCare: Immediate hospital trauma surgery, tetanus prophylaxis, and ongoing physical and psychosocial rehabilitation.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stop any bleeding with direct pressure, rinse the wound thoroughly with clean running water, and cover it with a clean dressing.
recognitionSigns: Superficial cut, scrape, graze, or small puncture on the skin without heavy gushing blood
Later infection signs: Increasing redness/purple-darkening, warmth, swelling, pus, or fever
steps: Wash your hands with soap and water (and put on disposable gloves if available).
Apply firm direct pressure with a clean cloth or gauze if the wound is bleeding until bleeding stops.
Rinse the wound thoroughly under clean (potable) lukewarm running tap water to flush out dirt (use sterile saline or povidone-iodine if clean tap water is unavailable).
Remove any remaining surface dirt gently with clean water and a sterile compress.
Pat the skin around the wound dry and cover the wound completely with a sterile plaster, hydrogel/hydrocolloid dressing, or clean bandage.

conditionalActions.condition: If no tap is available
conditionalActions.action: Pierce the cap of a clean, unused bottle of drinking water to squirt a gentle pressurized stream over the wound.

conditionalActions.condition: If bleeding is heavy or does not stop with pressure
conditionalActions.action: Switch immediately to Severe Bleeding steps and call 911.

conditionalActions.condition: If the wound later becomes hot, swollen, increasingly painful, red/darker, or the person develops a fever
conditionalActions.action: Do not cover an infected wound without care—seek medical evaluation promptly.

warnings: Avoid pouring harsh isopropyl rubbing alcohol or hydrogen peroxide into open wounds—they damage healthy tissue and cause unnecessary pain.
Do not leave fresh cuts exposed to dirt and air—covering a cleaned wound speeds healing.
Never pull out a deeply embedded object.
emergencyEscalation: Heavy or persistent bleeding (call 911)
Deep, gaping, or jagged wounds that may need stitches
Dirty or puncture wounds when tetanus vaccination is outdated (>5 years for dirty wounds, >10 years for clean wounds)
Signs of spreading skin infection or fever

learnMore.overview: Minor cuts, scrapes, and abrasions are everyday injuries that heal well when cleaned under pressurized potable water and kept covered. Proper wound cleaning and tetanus protection prevent serious bacterial infections.
causes: Falls onto rough surfaces, kitchen knives, sharp paper/metal edges, splinters, or thorns
riskFactors: Soil or rusty/dirty object contamination, unwashed hands, diabetes, or outdated tetanus immunization
detailedRecognition: Check the outside of the dressing daily: if clean and dry, leave it undisturbed; if stained with blood or fluid, remove gently, re-rinse with clean water, and apply a fresh dressing.
prevention: Wear protective gloves and footwear during manual work or sports, and handle sharp tools safely.
preparation: Stock adhesive plasters, sterile gauze pads, saline pods, and povidone-iodine in home and school first aid kits.
explanations: Cochrane evidence shows potable tap water cleans acute wounds as effectively as sterile saline for preventing infection.
Moist or protective dressings (plasters, film, hydrogel, hydrocolloid) reduce wound size and redness faster than leaving wounds uncovered.
additionalPrecautions: Cold packs wrapped in cloth can soothe minor closed bruising around a scrape.
followUpCare: Consult a doctor if redness spreads, pus appears, fever develops, or tetanus booster status is uncertain.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Pick up a knocked-out permanent tooth by the crown ONLY (never touch the root), store it moist in ORS, milk, or saliva-moistened clingfilm, and get to a dentist immediately.
recognitionSigns: A tooth has been completely knocked out of its socket after a fall, sports blow, or impact
Bleeding from the gum socket or lacerated lips/mouth
steps: Have the person press or bite gently on clean gauze or cotton over the empty gum socket to control bleeding.
Cover any sharp broken tooth edges in the mouth with gauze or cotton to protect lips and tongue.
Pick up a knocked-out permanent tooth by the white chewing crown ONLY—do NOT touch the root.

Store the uncleaned tooth immediately in oral rehydration salt (ORS) solution, balanced salt solution, or clingfilm moistened with the person's saliva (use cow's milk or a small cup of the person's saliva if those are unavailable).
Take the person and the stored tooth to a dentist or emergency clinic immediately, while checking for any head or facial injury.

conditionalActions.condition: If the knocked-out tooth is a young child's baby (milk) tooth
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT try to preserve it for replantation—control gum bleeding and see a dentist to check that no root fragment remains.

conditionalActions.condition: If signs of concussion or head trauma are present
conditionalActions.action: Prioritize airway and Head Injury / Spinal Injury care and call 911.

warnings: First aid providers must NEVER try to push or re-implant a knocked-out tooth back into the socket.
Do NOT scrub, rinse, or wipe the tooth root—delicate root cells needed for reattachment are easily destroyed.
Do NOT store a tooth in plain tap water, and do NOT let a child or dazed person hold a loose tooth inside their mouth (choking risk).
emergencyEscalation: Urgent dental care within minutes/hours is critical for successful permanent tooth re-implantation
Call 911 if facial impact caused brief unresponsiveness, heavy uncontrolled bleeding, jaw fracture, or airway compromise

learnMore.overview: Dental avulsion is the complete displacement of a tooth from its socket. A knocked-out adult (permanent) tooth can often be saved and re-implanted by a dentist if root cells are kept alive in an appropriate storage medium and dental care is reached rapidly.
causes: Contact sports, playground falls, bicycle/motorcycle crashes, or blows to the face
riskFactors: Playing contact sports without a mouthguard or riding bicycles/motorcycles without a helmet
detailedRecognition: Permanent teeth typically begin erupting around age 6; baby teeth in toddlers/preschoolers are not re-implanted because doing so can damage the developing permanent tooth underneath.
prevention: Wear fitted mouthguards during contact sports (basketball, boxing, martial arts) and helmets when cycling, skating, or riding motorcycles.
preparation: School clinics and sports coaches can keep small clean containers and ORS packets in first aid kits.
explanations: ILCOR systematic reviews show Hank's balanced salt solution, propolis, ORS solutions, rice water, clingfilm (with saliva), and cow's milk preserve root cell viability far better than tap water, which bursts root cells.
additionalPrecautions: Always maintain a clear airway first—mouth blood and loose teeth pose an aspiration risk in drowsy patients.
followUpCare: Follow dental splinting, antibiotic/tetanus, and soft-diet instructions after professional treatment.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Keep the blister intact (unpopped) whenever possible, wash gently with clean water, and cover it with a protective blister pad or dressing.
recognitionSigns: Small raised pocket of fluid on the foot, heel, toe, or palm after repetitive rubbing or walking
Localized tenderness or torn skin if the blister has burst
steps: Stop or adjust the rubbing activity (such as ill-fitting footwear or tool use) if possible.
Wash the blister and surrounding skin gently with clean water and soap, then pat dry.
Keep an intact blister unpopped and cover it with a cushioned blister plaster, moleskin, or clean non-stick dressing.
Clean a torn or self-drained blister under clean running water like a cut or graze, leave the loose skin flap in place, and cover with a sterile dressing.
Watch over the next several days for signs of infection (spreading redness, heat, pus, worsening pain, or fever).

conditionalActions.condition: If the person has diabetes, poor circulation, or a weakened immune system
conditionalActions.action: NEVER puncture the blister—protect it cleanly and seek medical advice promptly.

conditionalActions.condition: If a small intact blister (<=2 cm) causes severe pain preventing necessary walking (and the person is NOT diabetic)
conditionalActions.action: Disinfect the skin, carefully drain fluid while keeping the skin roof intact, and press a clean dressing over it.

warnings: NEVER peel or cut off the top skin layer ('deroofing') of a blister—the skin roof protects underlying tissue from bacteria.
Do NOT pop burn blisters or frostbite blisters.
Avoid sticky hydrocolloid blister plasters if the person must continue long-distance walking where repeated removal could tear fragile skin.
emergencyEscalation: Blisters in anyone with diabetes or immunocompromise
Large blisters (>2 cm) or blisters from burns, chemicals, or frostbite
Signs of infection: Increasing heat, spreading redness/darkening, pus, or fever

learnMore.overview: Friction blisters form when repetitive rubbing separates outer skin layers and fills the space with protective fluid. Leaving the blister intact preserves the body's natural sterile barrier against bacterial infection.
causes: Tight, loose, or damp shoes and socks during long walks/runs, or repetitive hand tool use
riskFactors: Moist sweaty skin, creased socks, grit inside shoes, unaccustomed long marches, or diabetes (high complication risk)
detailedRecognition: Early 'hot spots' feel warm and irritated before fluid accumulates—stopping to adjust socks/padding at this stage prevents full blisters.
prevention: Wear properly fitted, broken-in shoes and clean, dry moisture-wicking socks; wear work gloves when using tools.
preparation: Carry moleskin, sterile gauze, and surgical tape when hiking or walking long distances.
explanations: Controlled studies show keeping friction blisters intact significantly lowers Staphylococcus bacterial colonization compared with draining or removing the blister roof.
additionalPrecautions: Remove dressings slowly in sections while supporting the skin rather than ripping them off.
followUpCare: Seek medical care promptly if redness spreads, red streaks appear, or fever develops.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stop the burning source safely and cool thermal burns immediately under clean cool running water for at least 10 minutes—ideally 20 minutes.
recognitionSigns: Red/darkened, painful, blistered, or charred/pale leathery skin after contact with fire, hot liquid/steam, hot objects, electricity, or sun
Soot around mouth/nose, singed facial hair, hoarseness, or breathing difficulty (airway burn warning)
steps: Make the scene safe first: extinguish flames or turn off the electrical power source BEFORE touching an electrocuted person.
Cool thermal burns immediately with gentle, clean cool running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20 minutes.
Call 911 immediately if the burn is large, deep, on the face/mouth/throat/hands/feet/genitals, caused by electricity or flames, or involves a baby or vulnerable person.
Remove clothing, rings, watches, and jewellery near the burn BEFORE swelling starts—do NOT pull off anything stuck to the burned skin.
Cover the cooled burn loosely (do not wrap tightly) with a non-stick moist/hydrogel dressing, clean plastic cling wrap, or a clean wet cloth, placing moist sterile gauze between burned fingers.
Keep the rest of the person warm (especially babies, children, and older adults) to prevent hypothermia and shock while monitoring breathing.

conditionalActions.condition: If clean running water is unavailable
conditionalActions.action: Cool the burn using another clean cool liquid (such as bottled water, milk, or juice), pouring it over the burn rather than soaking in a warm stagnant bowl.

conditionalActions.condition: If the burn is mild sunburn
conditionalActions.action: Move into shade, offer cool fluids, apply aloe vera or aftersun lotion/gel, and seek medical care if extensive or in a baby.

conditionalActions.condition: If an electrocuted person is unresponsive and not breathing normally once power is off
conditionalActions.action: Start CPR immediately and send for an AED.

warnings: NEVER apply ice or ice-cold water directly to a burn—it worsens tissue damage and causes hypothermia.
NEVER burst burn blisters, and avoid applying butter, cooking oil, toothpaste, raw egg, or silver sulfadiazine cream.
Never touch someone still connected to live electricity.
emergencyEscalation: Large or deep burns, or any burn to the face, mouth/throat, hands, feet, major joints, or genitals
All electrical burns (internal heart/tissue injury can be severe even when skin marks look small)
Flame burns, smoke inhalation, or breathing difficulty
Burns in babies, young children, older adults, or people with diabetes

learnMore.overview: Heat continues damaging deeper skin layers even after the heat source is removed. Immediate cooling under clean running water for 10–20 minutes halts deeper tissue injury, reduces hospital stay, and eases pain.
causes: Hot liquids/steam (scalds), open flames, hot cooking oil/pans, electrical currents/lightning, or ultraviolet sun exposure
riskFactors: Floor-level cooking near toddlers, uninsulated electrical wiring, kerosene stoves, or prolonged midday sun exposure
detailedRecognition: Burns may look red, pale, purple, or darkened depending on skin tone and burn depth; deep burns destroy nerve endings and may feel surprisingly painless.
Large burns leak fluid from blood vessels and can rapidly cause circulatory shock.
prevention: Keep pot handles turned inward, supervise children away from stoves and hot liquids, inspect electrical cords, and use SPF >=30 sunscreen and shade.
preparation: Cool ONLY the burned area while keeping the rest of the person's body warm and dry, especially in children.
explanations: Plastic cling wrap laid lengthwise (not wrapped tightly around a limb) or hydrogel dressings keep burns clean, moist, and protected during hospital transport.
In resource-limited settings without sterile dressings, medical/clean honey or aloe vera may be used on minor cooled thermal burns.
additionalPrecautions: For chemical skin or eye burns, follow the dedicated Chemical Burns guide (continuous water flushing and strict self-protection).
followUpCare: Watch healing minor burns for signs of infection (increasing pain, warmth, spreading redness, pus, or fever) and seek medical care promptly.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Protect yourself from touching the chemical, then immediately flush the affected skin or eye continuously with clean running water until pain eases (at least 20 minutes) and call 911.
recognitionSigns: Stinging, burning pain, redness, blistering, or discolouration after contact with acid, alkali, bleach, lime, or industrial cleaners
Eye exposure: Intense eye pain, redness, tearing, eyelid spasm, or blurred vision
steps: Put on protective gloves/eyewear and avoid direct contact with the chemical or contaminated rinse water.
Brush off any dry powdered chemical gently (without touching it with bare skin) before wetting, and carefully remove contaminated clothing and jewellery.
Flush the burned skin or eye immediately with a gentle, continuous stream of clean (potable) running water (or sterile saline / Diphoterine if available) until pain eases—for at least 20 minutes.
Direct the rinse water away so diluted chemical runoff does NOT flow onto healthy skin or into the uninjured eye.
Remove contact lenses during eye rinsing if present, and call 911 or arrange urgent medical care.
Cover rinsed skin burns loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing or clean wet cloth while awaiting EMS.

conditionalActions.condition: If a chemical substance was swallowed
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT induce vomiting and do NOT give water or milk unless Poison Control or a medical professional instructs you—switch to Poisoning and call 911.

conditionalActions.condition: If the eye was splashed with a chemical
conditionalActions.action: Keep rinsing continuously en route if possible, do NOT apply eye drops or ointments, and never let the injured person drive themselves.

warnings: NEVER try to neutralize an acid with an alkali or vice versa—the chemical reaction generates heat that worsens the burn.
NEVER contaminate the uninjured eye while flushing an injured eye (tilt the head so the injured eye is lower).
Never touch contaminated clothing or chemicals with bare hands.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for all chemical eye exposures, large/deep chemical skin burns, facial/airway exposures, or swallowed chemicals

learnMore.overview: Corrosive acids and alkalis continue destroying skin and corneal eye tissue until completely washed away. Immediate, prolonged irrigation with potable running water (or Diphoterine where stocked) dramatically reduces full-thickness burns, eye surgeries, and vision loss.
causes: Household drain/oven cleaners, bleach, battery acid, cement/lime powder, agricultural pesticides, or laboratory/industrial chemicals
riskFactors: Handling cleaners or industrial agents without gloves and splash goggles, or storing chemicals in unmarked drink bottles
detailedRecognition: Alkalis (lime, cement, drain cleaner, ammonia) penetrate deeply and can cause progressive eye and skin destruction even if initial pain seems moderate.
prevention: Read product safety labels before use, wear protective gloves and eye shields, and store chemicals in original child-resistant containers.
preparation: Know the location of eyewash stations and safety showers in laboratories, workshops, and schools.
explanations: Observational studies show immediate tap-water irrigation of chemical eye and skin burns reduces severe burns, hospital stay, and corneal damage, with Diphoterine offering additional neutralizing wash benefit where available.
additionalPrecautions: Bring the chemical product name or container label (only if safe to handle in a sealed bag) to inform medical staff.
followUpCare: Ophthalmic evaluation is essential after any chemical eye splash to protect long-term vision.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Move the person out of bright/UV light immediately, advise removing contact lenses, and let their closed eyes rest.
recognitionSigns: Gritty feeling ('sand in the eyes'), burning pain, red watery eyes, and eyelid swelling hours after welding, sunlamp, water-glare, or high-altitude sun exposure
Painful sensitivity to light, blurred vision, or headache
steps: Move the person away from the UV light source into a dimly lit indoor space and reassure them.
Advise them to remove contact lenses gently if worn, and tell them NOT to rub their eyes.
Rest the eyes by keeping them closed as much as possible and wearing UV-filtering sunglasses if light causes discomfort.
Place a clean, cool damp cloth gently over the closed eyelids to soothe pain.
Use sterile saline solution or lubricating artificial-tear eye drops to keep the eyes moist.
Seek medical care if symptoms worsen or do not improve within 24 hours.

conditionalActions.condition: If vision loss is severe or a foreign metal spark/chemical entered the eye
conditionalActions.action: Do not rub or press on the eyeball—seek urgent medical/ophthalmic care immediately.

warnings: Do NOT rub the eyes—rubbing scratches the sunburned outer layer (cornea).
Do NOT instil unprescribed anaesthetic or steroid eye drops.
Never let someone with blurred vision or painful light sensitivity drive.
emergencyEscalation: Symptoms lasting longer than 24 hours or worsening pain
Severe or persistent loss of vision, pus/discharge, or suspected metal fragment from grinding/welding

learnMore.overview: Flash eye (photokeratitis, welder's arc eye, or snow blindness) is a painful ultraviolet (UV) burn of the cornea—similar to sunburn on the surface of the eye. Most cases heal within 24 hours when the eyes are rested and protected from further light.
causes: Welder's torches/arcs without proper welding shields, sunlamps/tanning beds, or intense UV reflection off water, white sand, snow, or high-altitude terrain
riskFactors: Welding or standing near welding without rated eye shields, or outdoor water/mountain activities without UV-blocking wraparound sunglasses
detailedRecognition: Pain and grittiness often appear several hours after the UV exposure rather than immediately.
prevention: Always wear certified welding helmets/goggles when welding and UV-filtering sunglasses with side protection on water, beaches, or mountains.
preparation: Keep sterile saline eye wash pods in workshop and outdoor kits.
explanations: Observational studies show protective eyewear significantly reduces work-related UV and flash eye injuries; corneal surface cells regenerate quickly when kept moist and rested.
additionalPrecautions: Wait until symptoms have completely resolved before wearing contact lenses again.
followUpCare: Consult an eye specialist if pain, redness, or blurred vision persists past 24 hours.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Keep the injured limb completely still in the position found—do NOT try to straighten or realign it—and seek medical care or call 911.
recognitionSigns: Deformity, abnormal angle, shortening/twisting of a limb, swelling, or bruising after a fall or blow
Severe pain, inability to move or bear weight, sound/feeling of a snap or grating bones, or bone protruding through skin
steps: Help the person keep the injured part still in the exact position found (let them support an injured arm against their chest if comfortable).
Control any bleeding first if it is an open fracture by pressing gently around protruding bone and covering with a clean dressing without pushing on the bone.
Support and stabilize the injury manually (with cushions, rolled clothing, or a sling) to prevent movement.
Apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth for up to 20 minutes on closed fractures to ease pain and swelling (remove if uncomfortable).
Call 911 immediately if the thigh (femur) or pelvis is injured, the bone broke through the skin, the limb is at an abnormal angle or pale/cold, pain is severe, or signs of shock appear.
Keep the person warm, record the time of injury, and avoid giving food or drink if surgery may be needed.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person MUST be transported a long distance over bumpy terrain
conditionalActions.action: Immobilize the limb gently with a padded splint in the position found to reduce jarring and pain.

conditionalActions.condition: If unsure whether an injury is a fracture, sprain, or strain
conditionalActions.action: Treat it as a fracture until an X-ray and medical professional confirm otherwise.

conditionalActions.condition: If neck or back injury is possible (fall from height or road crash)
conditionalActions.action: Do not move the person—follow Spinal Injuries care immediately.

warnings: NEVER try to straighten an angulated fracture or push a dislocated joint or protruding bone back into place.
NEVER place ice directly onto bare skin or leave ice on for more than 20 consecutive minutes.
Do not let someone walk on a suspected leg, ankle, or foot fracture ('being able to move it' does NOT rule out a broken bone).
emergencyEscalation: Open fractures (skin broken over the fracture) or suspected femur (thigh) / pelvic fractures
Abnormal limb angle, numbness/tingling, or pale, cold, pulseless hand/foot below the injury
Signs of circulatory shock or concurrent head/spinal injury

learnMore.overview: Fractures range from hairline cracks to major long-bone breaks and open fractures that cause life-threatening internal or external bleeding. Only an X-ray can reliably rule out a fracture, so any significant extremity injury should be stabilized in the position found.
causes: Falls, road traffic crashes, sports collisions, or direct blows/crush injuries
riskFactors: Osteoporosis, older age (falls), high-impact sports, or unsafe ladders/surfaces
detailedRecognition: Long-bone fractures—especially of the thigh bone (femur)—can bleed heavily inside the leg and trigger life-threatening shock even without an open skin wound.
Dislocations occur at joints (shoulder, elbow, finger, kneecap) and require the same immobilization and medical care as fractures.
prevention: Remove home trip hazards for older adults, stabilize ladders, wear seatbelts, and use protective sports gear.
preparation: Note that straightening an angulated fracture is restricted to specifically trained providers in remote settings when the distal limb is pale/cold or cannot be splinted for evacuation.
explanations: Stabilizing the bone in the position found prevents sharp bone ends from tearing nearby nerves, arteries, and muscles.
Wrapped cold application for up to 20 minutes helps numb acute pain without causing cold injury to skin.
additionalPrecautions: Remove rings or watches on an injured hand/arm early if safe to do so without moving the fracture, before swelling traps them.
followUpCare: All suspected fractures and dislocations require professional medical assessment and X-ray imaging.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stop the activity, rest and keep the injured joint still, and apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth for up to 20 minutes.
recognitionSigns: Pain, tenderness, swelling, or bruising around a joint (such as an ankle, knee, wrist, or finger) after twisting or falling
Pain or difficulty bearing weight or moving the joint
steps: Stop physical activity immediately and help the person rest—do NOT try to 'walk off' a sprain.
Support the injured joint in a comfortable, still position (resting it elevated if comfortable).
Apply ice or a cold pack wrapped in a cloth as soon as possible for up to 20 consecutive minutes to ease pain.
Apply a gentle compression bandage ONLY if it feels comfortable to the person, ensuring it is never tight enough to cause numbness, tingling, or colour change.
Seek medical evaluation if you cannot rule out a fracture—when in doubt, treat as a broken bone.

conditionalActions.condition: If pain returns after removing the cold pack
conditionalActions.action: Wait until skin temperature returns completely to normal before reapplying wrapped cold for up to 20 minutes.

conditionalActions.condition: If the joint looks deformed, heard a snap/grating, or has severe pain/inability to bear weight
conditionalActions.action: Immobilize in the position found and seek medical/X-ray care (or call 911 if severe) as a Fracture or Dislocation.

warnings: NEVER place ice directly on bare skin or cool continuously for longer than 20 minutes—cold burns/skin damage can occur.
Do NOT apply heat or alternating hot-and-cold packs to a fresh acute sprain.
Do NOT wrap a bandage tightly—remove immediately if toes or fingers feel numb, tingly, cold, or bluish.
emergencyEscalation: Visible joint deformity, abnormal limb angle, or suspected fracture/dislocation
Cold, pale, or numb fingers/toes below the injured joint
Severe pain, inability to bear weight, or lack of improvement over several days

learnMore.overview: A sprain occurs when tough ligament bands supporting a joint (most commonly the ankle, knee, or wrist) are overstretched or torn by a sudden twist. Because sprains and fractures look very similar without an X-ray, uncertain injuries should always be managed conservatively as potential fractures.
causes: Twisting an ankle on uneven ground or stairs, sports landings, or falling onto an outstretched hand
riskFactors: Previous joint sprains, uneven playing surfaces, improper footwear, or muscle fatigue
detailedRecognition: Rapid swelling, bruising, and localized joint pain are shared by both sprains and fractures—ability to move a joint slightly does NOT prove it is unbroken.
prevention: Wear supportive footwear suited to the activity, warm up before sports, and keep walkways well lit and clear.
preparation: Keep instant or reusable cold packs and clean cloth wraps accessible at sports venues and schools.
explanations: IFRC 2025 evidence reviews note that wrapped cooling up to 20 minutes can reduce acute pain, while routine tight compression or forced elevation lacks strong outcome evidence—comfort and avoiding circulation restriction come first.
additionalPrecautions: Avoid weight-bearing exercise initially; gentle non-weight-bearing mobilization may aid later recovery once acute pain subsides and fracture is excluded.
followUpCare: See a healthcare professional for X-ray or physiotherapy guidance if pain/swelling is significant or walking remains painful.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stop the activity immediately, rest the injured muscle in a comfortable position, and apply a cloth-wrapped cold pack for up to 20 minutes.
recognitionSigns: Sudden sharp or aching pain, tightness, cramping, swelling, or bruising in a muscle or tendon during lifting, sprinting, or stretching
Pain or weakness when contracting or stretching that muscle
steps: Have the person stop the activity immediately and rest—continuing exertion can turn a mild pull into a complete tear.
Support the injured limb or muscle in a comfortable, relaxed position that minimizes movement and tension.
Apply an ice pack or cold compress wrapped in a cloth as soon as possible for up to 20 minutes to reduce pain (stop if too uncomfortable).
Apply a light comfort wrap only if the person finds it soothing, ensuring circulation is never restricted.
Seek medical care if pain or swelling is severe, a pop/gap was felt in the muscle/tendon, or a fracture cannot be ruled out.

conditionalActions.condition: If the strain involves the lower back after lifting
conditionalActions.action: See Acute Lower Back Pain (or Spinal Injuries if caused by a fall or crash).

warnings: NEVER apply ice directly to bare skin or cool for more than 20 minutes at a time.
Do NOT massage deeply, stretch forcefully, or try to 'run off' a fresh muscle strain.
Avoid alternating heat and cold on a newly injured limb muscle—only wrapped cold is advised initially.
emergencyEscalation: Audible/felt 'pop' with complete inability to move a joint or bear weight (possible complete tendon rupture or fracture)
Severe swelling, numbness/tingling, or pale/cold extremity
Pain that worsens or fails to improve after several days of rest

learnMore.overview: A strain is an overstretching or tearing of muscle fibres or the tendon connecting muscle to bone—commonly affecting the hamstring, calf, thigh, shoulder, or back. Early rest, immobilization of painful motion, and short wrapped cooling limit further tearing and ease discomfort.
causes: Sudden sprinting or jumping, lifting heavy loads awkwardly, overstretching, or repetitive occupational strain
riskFactors: Fatigue, inadequate warm-up, previous muscle injury, or sudden bursts of unaccustomed exertion
detailedRecognition: Unlike sprains (centred on joint ligaments), strains cause tenderness and spasm along the muscle belly or tendon attachment—though near a joint, treat any doubtful injury as a potential fracture.
prevention: Condition muscles gradually, lift heavy loads by bending the knees with a straight back, and take rest breaks during repetitive work.
preparation: Keep cold packs and cloth wraps available during sports and physical training.
explanations: Early rest protects torn muscle fibres while initial healing begins; cooling for up to 20 minutes blunts acute pain signals without damaging skin.
additionalPrecautions: Wait for skin temperature to normalize completely before repeating a 20-minute cooling session.
followUpCare: Gradual, pain-free mobilization and medical/physiotherapy guidance help restore strength safely once acute pain settles.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 immediately and help the person stay completely still in the position found—do NOT move them or apply a neck collar.
recognitionSigns: Fall from greater than standing height, road crash, diving headfirst into shallow water, or crush/blast trauma
Neck or back pain/tenderness, tingling, numbness, or weakness/paralysis in arms, legs, or torso, or loss of bladder/bowel control
Head injury, altered consciousness, or intoxication after trauma (assume spinal injury)
steps: Call 911 immediately and tell EMS a spinal injury is suspected.
Reassure a responsive, alert person calmly and ask them to lie or stay completely still without turning their head.

Support the head gently with your hands (manual stabilization) to prevent movement if the person is a child, confused, drowsy, or unable to stay still—do NOT strap the head or apply a cervical collar.
Leave the person in the exact position found unless an immediate scene danger or blocked airway forces movement.
Keep the person warm (without moving their spine) to reduce shock, and monitor breathing and responsiveness continuously until EMS arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is unresponsive and breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Leave them in the position found, open the airway using a jaw thrust (preferred, less neck motion) or gentle head-tilt chin-lift while supporting the head still, and monitor breathing.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is unresponsive and NOT breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Airway and breathing take priority—carefully position on their back if needed and start CPR immediately.

conditionalActions.condition: If a pelvic fracture is suspected (severe hip/groin pain, inability to move legs)
conditionalActions.action: Keep them flat on their back with legs straight (pad gently between legs if trained), NEVER rock or press on the pelvis, and watch closely for shock.

warnings: First aid providers must NOT apply a cervical collar—evidence shows collars can cause harm and do not improve lay spinal stabilization.
NEVER move, sit up, or roll a suspected spinal casualty alone unless fire, water, or airway blockage threatens immediate death (use at least two helpers keeping head-neck-spine aligned).
Remember that some people with spinal fractures have NO initial numbness or paralysis—suspect it from the mechanism of injury.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately whenever a spinal or pelvic injury is suspected from trauma

learnMore.overview: Damage to the spinal cord can cause permanent paralysis or death, while life-saving airway and breathing care always take top priority. Keeping an alert casualty calm and still—or gently supporting the head manually without cervical collars—prevents secondary cord damage.
causes: Motor vehicle, motorcycle, or bicycle collisions, falls from ladders/roofs/trees, shallow-water diving, or contact-sport impacts
riskFactors: Adults over 65 or people with bone conditions (who can fracture the spine even from minor slips/falls), diving into murky/shallow water, or unrestrained vehicle travel
detailedRecognition: Young children and intoxicated or head-injured patients may not report neck pain—always protect the spine after high-risk trauma.
prevention: Wear seatbelts with properly adjusted headrests, wear helmets, stabilize ladders, and never dive headfirst into shallow or unfamiliar water.
preparation: Understand that manual in-line head support simply holds the head steady in neutral alignment without pulling or strapping.
explanations: ILCOR's 2025 scoping review of 66 spinal motion restriction studies reaffirmed the recommendation against cervical collar application by first aid providers.
Jaw thrust lifts the lower jaw forward to clear the tongue with less cervical spine movement than head-tilt chin-lift.
additionalPrecautions: Always check for concurrent Head Injury and Concussion.
followUpCare: EMS immobilization and hospital imaging are required to clear any suspected spinal injury.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Remove the person from their activity immediately, have them rest, and call 911 if any severe head-injury or concussion danger signs appear.
recognitionSigns: Forceful bump, blow, or jolt to the head or body causing rapid head movement
Mild signs: Scalp bump, mild headache, mild nausea, or feeling 'foggy'

Severe danger signs: Any loss of responsiveness (even brief), confusion/slurred speech/behaviour change, vomiting more than once, seizure, severe headache >2 hours, vision trouble, limb weakness/tingling, or blood/clear fluid from nose, ear, or mouth
steps: Stop the sport, work, or activity immediately and help the person rest—when in doubt, sit them out.
Screen for concussion: check if an impact/jolt occurred and whether there is any change in alertness, memory, balance, speech, mood, or vision.
Control any scalp bleeding with gentle direct pressure using a clean cloth (avoid pressing hard if a skull fracture is suspected).
Call 911 immediately and keep the head and neck completely still (assume Spinal Injury) if ANY severe danger sign is present.
Arrange medical evaluation by a healthcare professional for anyone with suspected concussion symptoms.
Observe even mildly bumped individuals over the next 24 hours (and ensuing days) for delayed danger signs.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 immediately, protect the neck/spine, maintain an open airway, and start CPR if breathing is absent or abnormal.

conditionalActions.condition: If a small scalp bump occurs with mild or no symptoms
conditionalActions.action: Apply a cloth-wrapped cold pack to the bump for up to 20 minutes, have them rest, and monitor closely for 24 hours.

warnings: NEVER allow an athlete, worker, or child with suspected concussion to return to sports, driving, or risky activity before full recovery and medical clearance.
Remember that life-threatening brain bleeding or concussion symptoms can develop hours after a head blow that initially seemed minor.
Always suspect a concurrent Spinal Injury after a fall from height, diving accident, or road crash.
emergencyEscalation: Becoming unresponsive, even for a few seconds
Confusion, agitation, slurred speech, seizure, or a child becoming unusually quiet/stopping play
Vomiting more than once, or severe headache lasting >2 hours despite pain relief
Blurred/double vision, light sensitivity, loss of balance, or limb tingling/weakness
Blood or clear watery fluid draining from the nose, ear, or mouth

learnMore.overview: Head injuries range from minor scalp bumps to concussions (traumatic brain injury) and life-threatening intracranial bleeding. Because no two concussions look identical and athletes/patients may downplay symptoms, immediate removal from activity and symptom-based screening are essential.
causes: Falls (especially toddlers and older adults), road crashes, contact sports, cycling accidents, or falling objects
riskFactors: Previous concussions, blood-thinning medications (high brain-bleed risk even after minor bumps), young age, or age >65
detailedRecognition: Three-question screen: (1) Did a potential injury occur? (2) Was the mechanism capable of head/brain jolt? (3) Was there any altered mental status? 'Yes' to all three requires immediate removal and EMS/medical evaluation.
In young children or people with dementia, watch for uncharacteristic crying, quietness, irritability, or refusal to play/eat.
prevention: Wear helmets on motorcycles, bicycles, and skateboards, use seatbelts, and remove household fall hazards.
preparation: Coaches, teachers, and parents should enforce 'if in doubt, sit them out' rules.
explanations: A second head impact before a concussion heals can cause catastrophic brain swelling; cognitive and physical rest allows the brain to recover.
additionalPrecautions: Avoid alcohol, sedatives, or unsupervised driving after a head injury.
followUpCare: Return to school, work, driving, and sports gradually only after all symptoms have resolved and a healthcare professional approves.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: First check whether a fall or crash caused the pain (if so, treat as Spinal Injury and call 911); for low-risk back strain, help them rest comfortably and apply a heat wrap.
recognitionSigns: Sudden aching or sharp pain in the lower back after lifting, twisting, or prolonged posture
Red-flag danger signs: Trauma/fall, pain shooting down a weak/numb leg, bladder or bowel problems, fever, or sudden inability to walk
steps: Check the cause first: if back pain followed a fall, car crash, or direct blow, stop—keep them completely still and follow Spinal Injuries care (call 911).
Comfort the person and help them sit or lie in whichever position feels most comfortable.
Apply a heat wrap, heating pad, or warm water bottle (wrapped in cloth) or a cold pack to the lower back for short-term pain relief.
Advise or assist with a recommended dose of over-the-counter painkiller (such as ibuprofen if no stomach/kidney/heart contraindications, or paracetamol per local rules).
Call 911 or seek urgent medical care if any red-flag neurological, trauma, or fever symptoms are present.

conditionalActions.condition: If leg weakness, numbness around the groin/buttocks, or bladder/bowel trouble occurs
conditionalActions.action: Seek emergency medical care immediately (possible spinal nerve compression).

warnings: Never treat trauma-related back pain as a simple muscle ache—always suspect Spinal Injury first.
Place a cloth barrier under heat pads/hot water bottles to avoid skin burns.
Be cautious with NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) in people with stomach ulcers, kidney disease, high blood pressure, or heart disease.
emergencyEscalation: Back pain caused by a fall, road crash, or direct trauma (call 911)
Weakness, numbness, or tingling in one or both legs, or sudden inability to walk
Bladder or bowel control problems, or sexual dysfunction
Back pain accompanied by fever, history of cancer, osteoporosis, weakened immunity, or long-term steroid use
Pain lasting 4 weeks or longer without improvement

learnMore.overview: Acute lower back pain from lifting or repetitive soft-tissue strain is very common in adults and usually improves over days to weeks. First aid focuses on ruling out serious spinal/nerve red flags, comfortable positioning, superficial heat therapy, and safe short-term analgesia.
causes: Muscle or ligament strain from heavy/awkward lifting, sudden twisting, or prolonged sitting/postures
riskFactors: Lifting heavy loads with straight knees and a bent back, physical inactivity, or repetitive manual work
detailedRecognition: Pain radiating down the back of one leg ('sciatica') or accompanied by leg weakness/bladder changes indicates nerve root compression needing medical evaluation.
prevention: Lift heavy objects by holding the load close, keeping your back straight, and pushing up with bent knees and stable legs.
Stay physically active with regular exercise and change positions regularly when working at a desk.
preparation: Combine regular exercise with safe lifting habits—evidence shows exercise + education lowers low-back pain risk better than back belts or shoe insoles alone.
explanations: Randomized trials show superficial heat wraps/packs significantly improve short-term pain relief and function in acute and subacute low back pain.
NSAIDs provide modest short-term relief, whereas paracetamol alone has limited effect in some studies but remains a guideline option depending on patient tolerances.
additionalPrecautions: Avoid prolonged strict bed rest once severe pain subsides; gentle movement aids recovery in uncomplicated back strain.
followUpCare: Consult a doctor if pain does not improve within 4 weeks or if new leg/nerve symptoms appear.

topics.title: Mammal Bites (Dog, Cat, Human & Animal Bites)

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Move safely away from the animal, stop any heavy bleeding, and immediately wash and flush the bite or scratch thoroughly with soap and clean running water.
recognitionSigns: Teeth marks, puncture wounds, torn skin, or scratches from a dog, cat, bat, monkey, other mammal, or human
Crushing/tearing wounds (common in dog bites) or deep narrow punctures (common in cat bites)
steps: Make sure the scene is safe and keep yourself and the injured person away from the animal.
Stop any heavy bleeding first with firm direct pressure (follow Severe Bleeding steps and call 911 if life-threatening).
Wash and flush the bite or scratch immediately and thoroughly with plenty of clean (potable) running water and soap (or sterile saline if soap/water is unavailable).
Pat the surrounding skin dry and cover the wound loosely with a clean, sterile dressing.
Send the person for prompt medical care TODAY to evaluate for rabies post-exposure vaccination, tetanus booster, antibiotics, or wound care.

conditionalActions.condition: If bitten or scratched in the Philippines or any rabies-endemic area (dog, cat, bat, stray, or wild mammal)
conditionalActions.action: Seek an Animal Bite Treatment Center or hospital immediately after soap-and-water washing for anti-rabies vaccination—rabies is fatal once symptoms start.

conditionalActions.condition: If a child is bitten on the face, head, or neck, or bleeding is severe
conditionalActions.action: Control bleeding with direct pressure and call 911 or go to an emergency department immediately.

warnings: NEVER skip thorough soap-and-water flushing—immediate washing physically removes saliva, bacteria, and rabies virus from the wound.
Do NOT apply garlic, vinegar, tandok, or unsterile folk poultices to animal bites, and do not tightly seal deep puncture wounds.
Do not try to chase or capture a stray or rabid-appearing animal yourself—report it to local authorities.
emergencyEscalation: Severe bleeding or deep tearing wounds, especially on a child's face or neck (call 911)
Any bite or scratch from a dog, cat, bat, monkey, or wild/stray mammal requiring urgent rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
Human bites that break the skin, deep cat-bite punctures (especially on hands), or outdated tetanus vaccination
Warmth, swelling, spreading redness, pus, or fever in the hours/days after a bite

learnMore.overview: Bites and scratches from dogs, cats, bats, monkeys, and humans carry high risks of bacterial wound infection, tetanus, and—critically in the Philippines—rabies. Immediate pressurized soap-and-water irrigation followed by prompt medical vaccination care saves lives.
causes: Domestic pets (young children are most often bitten on the face/neck by familiar animals; adults on hands/wrists), stray dogs/cats, bats, monkeys, or human fights
riskFactors: Approaching stray, eating, sleeping, or mothering animals; unsupervised young children around pets; unvaccinated animals
detailedRecognition: Cat bites create narrow, deep punctures that trap bacteria in joints/tendons and account for up to half of infected animal-bite injuries worldwide.
Even minor bat scratches or saliva contact with broken skin require rabies evaluation.
prevention: Vaccinate pet dogs and cats against rabies, supervise babies and children around all animals, and never approach stray or wild animals.
preparation: Know the nearest City Health Office / Animal Bite Treatment Center for prompt rabies and tetanus prophylaxis.
explanations: Potable running water and soap mechanically flush bacteria and inactivate enveloped viruses such as rabies in the wound.
Note that povidone-iodine has no proven advantage over thorough soap-and-water or saline irrigation for animal bites.
additionalPrecautions: Offer calm emotional reassurance, especially to frightened children after an animal attack.
followUpCare: Complete the full prescribed schedule of anti-rabies/tetanus shots and monitor the bite daily for redness, heat, or swelling.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Check immediately for severe allergic reaction or mouth/throat swelling (call 911 if present); scrape out a bee stinger with a flat card or pull a tick straight out with fine tweezers.
recognitionSigns: Sharp stinging pain, raised red/darkened bump (weal), localized swelling, or itching
Attached bee stinger or attached pinhead-to-pea-sized tick in the skin
Danger signs: Sting inside mouth/throat, wheezing, swollen tongue/lips, widespread hives, or dizziness (Anaphylaxis)
steps: Call 911 immediately if stung inside the mouth/throat (give ice to suck if alert) or if any signs of Anaphylaxis appear (assist with epinephrine autoinjector if prescribed).
Remove a bee stinger as quickly as possible by gently scraping across the skin with a flat edge (such as a bank card or blunt butter knife).
Remove an attached tick by grasping it as close to the skin as possible with fine tweezers (or a commercial tick tool) and pulling steadily and firmly straight out.
Wash the bite or sting thoroughly with clean water and soap (or an antiseptic solution if clean water is unavailable).
Remove rings/watches on a stung hand, apply a cold pack (ice in a cloth/bag) to reduce pain and swelling, and advise not to scratch.

conditionalActions.condition: If removing a tick
conditionalActions.action: Write down the date and body area bitten, and seek medical care if a rash (including a circular/ringed rash, or purplish/yellowish patch on darker skin), fever, headache, or joint pain develops.

conditionalActions.condition: If attacked by a swarm of bees or wasps
conditionalActions.action: Run immediately to indoor shelter (do not swat wildly or jump into water).

warnings: Avoid pinching a bee stinger with tweezers or fingers—squeezing the venom sac can inject more venom.
NEVER apply gasoline, petroleum jelly, nail polish, alcohol, ice, or a lit match/heat to a tick, and do not crush its body.
Remember that rashes look less bright red on brown or black skin—check lighter areas (palms/soles) and watch for swelling or systemic symptoms.
emergencyEscalation: Any signs of Anaphylaxis (difficulty breathing, throat/tongue swelling, dizziness/collapse)—call 911 immediately
Bite or sting inside the mouth or on the throat (airway swelling risk)—call 911 immediately
Multiple stings, stinger stuck deep, worsening pain/swelling after 24–48 hours, or fever/rash after a tick or mosquito bite

learnMore.overview: Most insect bites and stings cause temporary local pain and itching, but bee/wasp stings can trigger rapid anaphylaxis, mouth stings can block the airway, and ticks and mosquitoes can transmit serious infections.
causes: Bees, wasps, hornets, fire ants, mosquitoes, and ticks
riskFactors: Known venom allergy, walking barefoot on flowering grass, open sweet drinks outdoors, or walking in tick/mosquito-endemic areas
detailedRecognition: Ticks are painless when biting and start pinhead-small before swelling to pea-size.
Fever after mosquito bites in tropical regions like the Philippines requires medical evaluation for dengue or malaria.
prevention: Use DEET/approved insect repellent and mosquito nets, cover outdoor food/drinks, wear shoes on grass, shake out shoes/clothes, and never disturb hives.
preparation: Ensure anyone with a known insect-venom allergy carries their prescribed epinephrine autoinjector.
explanations: Quick removal of a bee stinger reduces venom delivery and weal size; fine tweezers or commercial tick tools remove ticks cleanly with minimal mouthpart breakage, whereas chemicals/heat/freezing fail to detach ticks.
additionalPrecautions: Keep fingernails clean and avoid scratching bites to prevent secondary bacterial skin infection.
followUpCare: Seek medical advice if redness/purple darkening, warmth, pus, fever, or flu-like illness develops.

topics.title: Aquatic Animal Injuries (Jellyfish, Stingray & Sea Urchin)

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 immediately for deadly species (such as box jellyfish) or breathing/allergy trouble; protect your hands, remove tentacles, rinse jellyfish stings with SEAWATER, and immerse in hot water (40–45°C) for 20–30 minutes.
recognitionSigns: Immediate burning/stinging pain, red/darkened whip-like welts, or tentacles clinging to skin (jellyfish)
Intense sharp pain, bleeding puncture/laceration, or brittle spines in the foot/leg (stingray or sea urchin)
Danger signs: Difficulty breathing, chest pain, muscle cramps, collapse, or Anaphylaxis
steps: Move the person safely out of the water and call 911 immediately if a deadly species (such as box jellyfish) is suspected or if breathing difficulty, severe pain, or allergic signs occur.
Protect your hands (gloves, tweezers, or a towel) and remove visible jellyfish tentacles with tweezers, or coat stinging cells with sand/shaving foam and scrape off gently with a bank card/cardboard.
Rinse a jellyfish sting thoroughly with SEAWATER (do NOT rinse with fresh water).

Relieve pain from non-life-threatening jellyfish or venomous fish stings by immersing or showering the stung area in hot water (40–45°C / 104–113°F—hot enough to relieve pain without burning healthy skin) for 20 to 30 minutes, or apply a heat pack.
Remove visible surface spines from sea urchin or sea star injuries and wash those puncture wounds thoroughly with soap and clean fresh water.
Monitor airway, breathing, and allergic reactions closely, and seek medical care for tetanus protection, spines near/in a joint, or persistent pain.

conditionalActions.condition: If stung by a confirmed box jellyfish and 5% vinegar is immediately available
conditionalActions.action: Flooding with vinegar for 30–60 seconds may prevent undischarged box-jellyfish cells from firing; otherwise rinse thoroughly with seawater (never use vinegar on Portuguese Man O' War / bluebottle stings where effects conflict).

conditionalActions.condition: If hot water or a heat pack is unavailable for jellyfish pain
conditionalActions.action: Apply a dry cold pack (not cold fresh water directly on skin) to ease pain.

warnings: NEVER rinse a jellyfish sting with fresh water, alcohol, ammonia, or meat tenderizer, and NEVER rub the stung skin—these trigger remaining stinging cells to fire more venom.
Test hot water on uninjured skin first (maximum 45°C / 113°F) so you do not scald the person.
Never touch beached/dead jellyfish with bare hands—their tentacles can still sting.
emergencyEscalation: Suspected box jellyfish or other deadly marine envenomation—call 911 immediately and prepare for CPR if unresponsive
Any signs of Anaphylaxis, breathing difficulty, chest pain, or altered consciousness
Stingray lacerations, sea urchin spines embedded in a joint, or signs of wound infection/tetanus risk

learnMore.overview: Jellyfish tentacles carry microscopic stinging capsules (nematocysts), while stingrays, venomous fish, and sea urchins inflict painful spine wounds. Seawater rinsing prevents extra jellyfish venom discharge, and controlled 40–45°C hot-water immersion inactivates heat-sensitive marine toxins to relieve pain.
causes: Jellyfish (including dangerous box jellyfish in Philippine/Indo-Pacific waters), stingrays, stonefish/weever fish, sea urchins, and crown-of-thorns starfish
riskFactors: Swimming during jellyfish season without rashguards/protective suits, or wading barefoot over reefs and sandy shallows
detailedRecognition: Box jellyfish stings can cause rapid cardiovascular collapse and cardiac arrest within minutes, requiring immediate EMS and CPR readiness.
prevention: Heed local beach warning signs, wear protective swim shirts/leggings and reef footwear, and shuffle feet gently in stingray-prone shallows.
preparation: Beach clinics and boaters can keep tweezers, protective gloves, and safe warm-water/heat-pack supplies ready.
explanations: ILCOR 2025 systematic reviews strongly recommend seawater rinsing for jellyfish stings and suggest 40–45°C heated water/heat packs over cold packs, alcohol, or ammonia for non-life-threatening jellyfish pain.
Pressure immobilization bandages are NOT recommended for jellyfish stings.
additionalPrecautions: Watch puncture wounds over the ensuing days for bacterial infection (warmth, redness/darkening, swelling, pus, fever).
followUpCare: Ensure tetanus immunization is current and seek medical removal for deep or joint-penetrating spines.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Move safely away from the snake, call 911 immediately, and keep the person lying down as completely still as possible to slow venom spread.
recognitionSigns: Fang puncture marks or scratch, localized pain, swelling, or bruising/discolouration
Systemic venom signs: Nausea/vomiting, blurred/double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, tingling/paralysis, drooling, sweating, bleeding, seizures, or shock
steps: Move the person and yourself to a safe spot well away from the snake—do NOT try to catch, chase, or kill the snake.

Help the person lie down comfortably, keep the bitten limb at or slightly below heart level, and instruct them to stay as still as possible (support a bitten arm in a sling; do NOT let them walk on a bitten leg).
Call 911 immediately and arrange rapid transport to a hospital equipped with antivenom.
Remove rings, watches, bracelets, and tight clothing near the bitten limb gently BEFORE swelling starts, moving the limb as little as possible.
Mark the leading edge of swelling on the skin if possible and note the exact time of the bite for hospital staff.
Calm and reassure the person while monitoring breathing, alertness, and signs of shock continuously until EMS takes over.

conditionalActions.condition: If safe from a distance, note the snake's appearance or take a quick photo
conditionalActions.action: Share the description/photo with hospital doctors—but NEVER delay care or risk another bite to identify the snake.

conditionalActions.condition: If in a remote/wilderness setting with long EMS wait times
conditionalActions.action: Gently wash the wound with clean water and immobilize the limb with a splint/non-elastic wrap without restricting blood flow (pressure immobilization with pad + non-elastic bandage is ONLY for specifically trained providers in special remote contexts).

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally (neurotoxic paralysis/arrest)
conditionalActions.action: Start CPR with rescue breaths immediately.

warnings: NEVER apply a tourniquet to a snakebite—tourniquets worsen tissue destruction, local swelling, and hospital stay without saving life.
NEVER cut the wound with a blade, NEVER suck out venom, NEVER apply ice/cold packs, NEVER rub the bite, and NEVER rely on 'black stone' or charcoal.
Even non-venomous snakebites require medical care for infection and tetanus risk.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 / transport urgently to a hospital for EVERY snakebite—antivenom and airway support in hospital are the definitive life-saving treatments

learnMore.overview: Snake venom travels primarily through lymphatic vessels driven by muscle movement. Keeping the bitten person calm, lying down, and completely still slows venom spread while urgent hospital transport for antivenom is arranged.
causes: Defensive bites when stepping near, reaching into grass/brush/firewood, or disturbing venomous or non-venomous snakes
riskFactors: Walking barefoot or in sandals at night/in tall grass, farming/forestry work, or attempting to handle/kill snakes
detailedRecognition: Neurotoxic venoms (such as Philippine cobras) can cause progressive eyelid drooping, difficulty swallowing, and breathing paralysis with minimal local swelling, whereas viper venoms cause intense swelling and bleeding.
prevention: Wear closed boots and long trousers in grassy/wooded areas, use a flashlight at night, and step away calmly without disturbing any snake encountered.
preparation: Know which regional hospitals stock antivenom.
explanations: Evidence summaries (CEBaP/ILCOR) strongly recommend against tourniquets, suction, cryotherapy (ice), and incision because they increase tissue necrosis and hospital complications without removing venom.
Rest and limb immobilization measurably slow lymphatic venom transit.
additionalPrecautions: Carry the person on a stretcher or vehicle rather than letting them walk.
followUpCare: Hospital observation, antivenom evaluation, tetanus prophylaxis, and wound infection monitoring are required.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Ensure your own safety from fumes/chemicals, stop further exposure, NEVER induce vomiting, and call 911 or Poison Control immediately.
recognitionSigns: Open pill bottles, household cleaners, pesticides, button batteries, or gas fumes nearby
Burns around mouth/lips, chemical smell on breath, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, seizures, or difficulty breathing
steps: Check scene safety first—do NOT enter a room or tank filled with toxic gas/fumes without rescue protection, and prevent any flames, sparks, or electrical switches if gas is suspected.
Stop further exposure safely: move from toxic air to fresh air if safe, or let a responsive person rinse residual liquid poison from their mouth with water and SPIT IT OUT.
Identify what substance was taken, how much, and when (touch containers only if safe).
Call 911 (or Poison Control) immediately, report all details, and follow their exact instructions.
Help a responsive person who swallowed poison rest comfortably on their LEFT side if possible, and monitor breathing and alertness continuously.
Gather pill bottles, chemical containers, or labels safely to hand to arriving EMS.

conditionalActions.condition: If a child or adult may have swallowed a button (coin) battery
conditionalActions.action: Treat as an immediate medical emergency—go to an emergency hospital/call 911 at once for an urgent X-ray, as lithium coin batteries can burn through the oesophagus within 2 hours.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Start CPR immediately—if corrosive chemicals, cyanide, hydrogen sulphide, or organophosphate pesticides are on/around the mouth, perform chest-compression-only CPR to protect yourself.

conditionalActions.condition: If opioid overdose is suspected
conditionalActions.action: Follow Suspected Opioid Overdose steps (CPR + naloxone if available).

warnings: NEVER make the person vomit (no fingers in throat, salt water, or ipecac)—corrosives and hydrocarbons cause severe internal burns and lung damage if vomited.
Do NOT give milk, water, or activated charcoal to swallow UNLESS Poison Control or a doctor specifically tells you to do so.
Remember carbon monoxide gas is completely odourless, colourless, and tasteless—suspect it if multiple people in a closed space develop headache, nausea, dizziness, or collapse.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for unresponsiveness, breathing difficulty, seizures, intentional overdose, corrosive ingestion, toxic gas inhalation, or swallowed button batteries

learnMore.overview: Poisons can damage the body rapidly when swallowed, inhaled, or absorbed through skin or eyes. Rapid identification of the substance, stopping exposure safely, avoiding harmful home remedies like induced vomiting, and contacting EMS/Poison Control are critical.
causes: Household cleaners/bleach/kerosene, medications, pesticides, carbon monoxide from generators/heaters/charcoal in closed spaces, button batteries, e-cigarette liquids, or alcohol/hand-sanitizer ingestion in young children
riskFactors: Children under 5 years (curiosity, colourful pods/bottles/button batteries), unmarked drink containers used for chemicals, or unventilated fuel appliances
detailedRecognition: Poisoning can mimic stroke, seizure, or low blood sugar.
Carbon monoxide victims rarely look blue (cyanotic) despite severe oxygen deprivation.
prevention: Lock all medicines, cleaners, pesticides, hand sanitizers, and spare button batteries in child-resistant containers out of reach of children, and never run generators or charcoal stoves indoors.
preparation: Keep local emergency numbers (911 and hospital poison centre contacts) posted at home and work.
explanations: Controlled studies show resting in the left lateral position slows stomach emptying into the intestine, reducing early absorption of several swallowed drugs while keeping the airway safer if vomiting occurs.
Cochrane reviews confirm induced vomiting (ipecac) and unsupervised activated charcoal provide no lay first aid benefit and can cause serious harm.
additionalPrecautions: If chemicals splashed onto skin or eyes, switch immediately to continuous water flushing under Chemical Burns.
followUpCare: Medical observation is essential because many poisons have delayed organ effects hours after ingestion.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Have the person sit upright, lean their head slightly forward, and pinch the soft lower part of their nostrils continuously for 10 to 15 minutes.
recognitionSigns: Blood dripping or flowing from one or both nostrils, spontaneously or after a bump to the nose
Taste or trickle of blood running down the back of the throat
steps: Reassure the person (especially young children) and help them sit upright leaning slightly forward—do NOT let them tilt their head back or lie flat.
Pinch the soft lower third of the nose firmly shut against the septum using thumb and index finger continuously for 10 to 15 minutes without peeking.
Instruct them to breathe calmly through their mouth and spit out any blood that drains into the throat rather than swallowing it.
Release pressure slowly after 10 to 15 minutes; if bleeding continues, pinch again for one more 10-to-15-minute period and seek medical care if it still does not stop.
Call 911 or seek urgent medical care immediately if the person feels faint/dizzy from heavy blood loss, takes blood thinners, or has signs of head/facial trauma.

conditionalActions.condition: If the nosebleed followed a blow to the head or face with nasal deformity or concussion signs (confusion, vomiting, blurred vision, clear watery fluid)
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT force-pinch a deformed broken nose or pack the nostrils—call 911 immediately and manage as a Head Injury.

conditionalActions.condition: If the nosebleed occurs in a child under 2 years old
conditionalActions.action: Arrange medical evaluation with a doctor even if bleeding stops.

warnings: NEVER tilt the head backward—blood running down the throat can block the airway or irritate the stomach and cause vomiting.
Do NOT apply ice packs (cryotherapy) to the forehead, neck, or nose—evidence does not support cryotherapy for stopping acute nosebleeds.
Avoid nose-picking, rubbing, or forceful nose-blowing after bleeding stops.
emergencyEscalation: Bleeding continues after 15 minutes of continuous firm pinching (or after two 10–15 minute cycles)
Person feels lightheaded, dizzy, pale, or weak from blood loss
Person takes anticoagulant/antiplatelet blood thinners (such as warfarin or aspirin) or has a clotting disorder (such as haemophilia)
Nosebleed after trauma with suspected brain injury, facial fracture, or nasal deformity (call 911)

learnMore.overview: Nosebleeds (epistaxis) usually come from fragile surface blood vessels in the front lower part of the nasal septum. Direct continuous manual compression of the soft nostrils while leaning slightly forward stops almost all uncomplicated nosebleeds.
causes: Dry or hot air, allergies, colds, nose-picking or forceful blowing, minor bumps, or blood-thinning medications
riskFactors: Children and adults aged 10–60, dry climates/air conditioning, anticoagulant therapy, or clotting disorders
detailedRecognition: Watery or blood-tinged clear fluid dripping from the nose after a serious head blow can be cerebrospinal fluid from a skull-base fracture—treat immediately as a severe Head Injury.
prevention: Avoid nose-picking and forceful blowing, and wear protective faceguards during contact sports.
preparation: Use a clock or phone timer to maintain steady 10–15 minute pressure—releasing every minute to check restarts bleeding.
explanations: Pinching the bony bridge of the nose does nothing; pressure must compress the soft lower third of the nostrils.
ILCOR's scoping review found insufficient clinical evidence to recommend ice/cryotherapy for acute nosebleeds, keeping direct soft-nostril pressure as the primary intervention.
additionalPrecautions: Wear gloves or have the person pinch their own nose to prevent blood exposure.
followUpCare: See a doctor if nosebleeds recur frequently within a month.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 immediately, stop all physical activity, help the person sit comfortably, and assist with 150–500 mg chewable aspirin if not allergic or contraindicated.
recognitionSigns: Squeezing, heavy, crushing, or burning pain/pressure in the centre or left side of the chest
Pain spreading to one or both arms, neck, jaw, back, or upper stomach
Shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea, dizziness, pale skin, or sudden extreme fatigue (common in women, older adults, and people with diabetes)
steps: Call 911 immediately at the first suspicion of cardiac chest pain—do not wait to see if symptoms pass.
Stop all physical exertion and help the person rest in a comfortable semi-sitting position (back supported, knees bent) with tight clothing loosened.
Assist the person to take their own prescribed angina medication (such as sublingual nitroglycerin) if they carry it.

Encourage a conscious adult to chew and swallow 150–500 mg of plain, non-enteric-coated aspirin ONLY if local rules permit and they have no aspirin allergy, active bleeding, bleeding disorder, or medical advice against it.
Send someone to fetch the nearest AED so it is ready beside you.
Reassure the person calmly and monitor responsiveness and breathing continuously until EMS arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally (or only gasps)
conditionalActions.action: Start CPR immediately and attach/use the AED as soon as available.

conditionalActions.condition: If chest pain looks like indigestion, back ache, or unusual fatigue in a woman, older adult, or person with diabetes
conditionalActions.action: Treat as possible cardiac chest pain and call 911 immediately.

warnings: Do NOT let the person walk, exert themselves, or drive themselves to the hospital.
Do NOT give aspirin to anyone allergic to aspirin, under 16 years, actively bleeding, or advised by a doctor not to take it, and never delay calling 911 to search for aspirin.
Do NOT administer routine supplemental oxygen in uncomplicated chest pain unless trained and clear hypoxia is present.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for any sudden unexplained chest pain, tightness, or suspected heart attack, or angina pain not relieved within a few minutes of rest/prescribed spray

learnMore.overview: Cardiac chest pain occurs when blood flow to heart muscle is severely reduced or blocked (acute coronary syndrome / heart attack). Rapid EMS activation, complete rest, early chewable aspirin, and immediate AED readiness save heart muscle and prevent fatal cardiac arrest.
causes: Coronary artery blockage by plaque rupture and blood clot (myocardial infarction) or temporary narrowing (angina)
riskFactors: High blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity, physical inactivity, older age, or family history of heart disease
detailedRecognition: Women, older adults, and people with diabetes frequently experience atypical symptoms—shortness of breath, nausea/vomiting, jaw/back ache, or sudden exhaustion—without classic crushing chest pain.
prevention: Control blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol, avoid tobacco, stay physically active, and keep prescribed angina medicine accessible.
preparation: Know the location of nearby public AEDs and emergency numbers (911, Red Cross 143).
explanations: Chewing 150–500 mg non-coated aspirin allows rapid bloodstream absorption to inhibit platelet clumping so the coronary clot stops growing.
Resting semi-upright reduces the heart's oxygen demand and eases breathing.
additionalPrecautions: Verify carefully that nitroglycerin belongs to the person and ask if they took erectile dysfunction medication (such as sildenafil), which makes nitrates dangerous.
followUpCare: Immediate hospital ECG, blood troponin testing, and coronary reperfusion therapy are essential even if chest discomfort temporarily eases.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Check FAST (Face, Arms, Speech, Time), note the exact time symptoms started, and call 911 immediately.
recognitionSigns: Face: One side of the face droops or feels numb when asked to smile
Arms: One arm drifts downward or cannot be raised equally with the other
Speech: Speech is slurred, strange, or confused, or the person cannot understand simple words
Sudden severe headache, sudden loss of balance/dizziness, or sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes
steps: Perform the FAST check right away: ask the person to smile (Face), raise both arms (Arms), and repeat a simple phrase (Speech).
Call 911 immediately if ANY single FAST sign or sudden neurological symptom is present (Time is brain).
Record the exact time symptoms began—or the last time the person was seen completely normal—to report to EMS.
Help a responsive person rest comfortably (lying on their back with head and shoulders slightly supported if comfortable) and keep them calm.
Give NOTHING to eat, drink, or swallow (no water, food, or aspirin), because stroke often impairs swallowing.
Monitor responsiveness and breathing closely until EMS arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If symptoms disappear completely within minutes (suspected TIA / mini-stroke)
conditionalActions.action: Still call 911 or seek emergency hospital assessment immediately—a full stroke frequently follows soon after.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is unresponsive or drooling heavily but breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Place them on their side in the recovery position to protect the airway.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Start CPR immediately.

warnings: NEVER give aspirin for a suspected stroke—a bleeding (haemorrhagic) stroke looks identical to a clot stroke and aspirin will worsen brain bleeding.
NEVER give food or drink—choking and aspiration risk is very high.
Do NOT administer routine supplemental oxygen in suspected stroke unless trained and hypoxia is confirmed.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for any positive FAST sign, sudden numbness/weakness, sudden vision/balance loss, thunderclap headache, or resolved TIA symptoms

learnMore.overview: A stroke occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is blocked by a clot (ischaemic stroke) or when a brain blood vessel bursts (haemorrhagic stroke). Millions of brain cells die every minute until hospital treatment restores blood flow or controls bleeding.
causes: Cerebral artery blood clot/embolism (~85%) or ruptured cerebral blood vessel (~15%)
riskFactors: High blood pressure, atrial fibrillation (irregular heartbeat), smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, prior TIA, or older age (though stroke can occur at any age)
detailedRecognition: Extended signs (BE-FAST) also include sudden Balance loss/vertigo and sudden Eyesight loss or double vision.
If the person has known diabetes and access to a blood glucose meter without delaying EMS, checking blood sugar helps distinguish severe hypoglycemia from stroke.
prevention: Monitor and treat high blood pressure and irregular heart rhythms, stop smoking, stay active, and eat a balanced low-salt diet.
preparation: Teach everyone in your household and school the FAST test (Face, Arms, Speech, Time).
explanations: Clot-busting drugs and mechanical clot removal only work within strict time windows measured from the exact minute symptoms started (or last seen normal).
Only a hospital CT/MRI brain scan can tell a clot stroke from a bleeding stroke, which is why aspirin is strictly avoided before scanning.
additionalPrecautions: Speak calmly and clearly even if the person cannot speak back—they may still hear and understand everything you say.
followUpCare: Urgent stroke-unit admission, brain imaging, swallowing assessment, and early rehabilitation.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Assist with an epinephrine (adrenaline) autoinjector into the outer mid-thigh immediately, call 911, and keep the person lying down (or sitting upright if struggling to breathe).
recognitionSigns: Sudden airway/breathing trouble: swollen tongue, lips, or throat, hoarse voice, noisy wheezing/stridor, or persistent cough
Circulation signs: pale clammy skin, dizziness, fainting, confusion, or collapse
Often combined with widespread hives/rash, flushing, or sudden vomiting/abdominal cramps after food, sting, or medicine exposure
steps: Help the person use their prescribed epinephrine (adrenaline) autoinjector immediately—press firmly into the outer mid-thigh (through light clothing if needed, avoiding seams/pockets) and hold per device instructions.
Call 911 immediately and tell the dispatcher 'suspected anaphylaxis'.
Remove any obvious trigger safely (such as scraping away a bee stinger or stopping food intake) without delaying epinephrine.
Position safely: keep the person lying flat on their back (legs raised if dizzy/pale), OR help them sit upright leaning forward if breathing is difficult—NEVER let them stand or walk.
Give a second epinephrine autoinjector dose into the outer thigh if symptoms do not improve or worsen after 5–10 minutes.
