Stay with the person and monitor airway, breathing, and alertness continuously until EMS arrives, even if they feel completely recovered.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is vomiting or unresponsive while breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Place them on their side in the recovery position (and place a visibly pregnant person on her left side).

conditionalActions.condition: If you are unsure whether symptoms are asthma or anaphylaxis in someone with severe allergy
conditionalActions.action: Give the epinephrine autoinjector FIRST, then their asthma reliever inhaler.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Start CPR immediately.

warnings: NEVER make a person with anaphylaxis stand up or walk—sudden posture change can trigger fatal blood-pressure collapse within seconds.
NEVER rely on oral antihistamines or asthma inhalers alone to treat anaphylaxis—only epinephrine reverses airway swelling and shock.
Do NOT inject epinephrine into hands, feet, buttocks, or veins—always use the outer mid-thigh.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 and go to the hospital EVERY time anaphylaxis occurs or epinephrine is used, because a second (biphasic) reaction can recur hours later

learnMore.overview: Anaphylaxis is a rapid, life-threatening systemic allergic reaction affecting breathing and/or circulation. Immediate intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline) in the outer mid-thigh is safe, life-saving, and must never be delayed.
causes: Foods (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, milk, eggs, sesame), insect venom (bees, wasps, ants), medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs), or latex
riskFactors: Previous anaphylaxis, co-existing poorly controlled asthma, teenagers/young adults eating away from home, or delayed epinephrine use
detailedRecognition: Skin hives or swelling are absent in up to 10–20% of anaphylaxis cases—sudden breathing difficulty or collapse after exposure to a likely allergen is enough to treat as anaphylaxis.
prevention: Strictly check food/medicine labels, wear medical-alert identification, and carry two in-date epinephrine autoinjectors at all times.
preparation: Practise with a trainer autoinjector device and share written allergy action plans with schools, family, and coworkers.
explanations: Epinephrine rapidly constricts leaky blood vessels to restore blood pressure, relaxes bronchial muscles to open airways, and reduces throat swelling.
Biphasic reactions can recur up to 72 hours (rarely up to 78 hours) after initial recovery without new allergen exposure, requiring hospital observation.
additionalPrecautions: Record the exact time each autoinjector dose was given and hand used devices safely to EMS.
followUpCare: Hospital observation, replacement of used autoinjectors before discharge, and specialist allergy review.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Remove or move away from the allergen, check carefully that breathing and alertness are completely normal, soothe local symptoms, and watch closely for any progression to anaphylaxis.
recognitionSigns: Itchy skin, raised red/skin-coloured welts (hives), or mild localized lip/face swelling WITHOUT airway or breathing difficulty
Sneezing, itchy/watery eyes, or runny/blocked nose
Normal voice, normal breathing, and no dizziness or faintness
steps: Confirm there are NO signs of anaphylaxis (no noisy/difficult breathing, throat/tongue swelling, hoarse voice, persistent cough, or dizziness).
Help the person stop exposure to the trigger (wash skin with cool water if contact allergen, or move away from pollen/dust/pets).
Rinse itchy eyes or nasal passages gently with sterile saline if eye/nose allergy symptoms are present.
Apply a cool damp cloth or plain fragrance-free moisturizer/emollient to soothe itchy hives or skin rash.
Assist the person to take their own oral non-sedating antihistamine ONLY if local rules permit and they have no contraindications.
Observe the person closely for at least 1–2 hours to ensure symptoms do not escalate into anaphylaxis.

conditionalActions.condition: If ANY breathing difficulty, throat tightness, tongue swelling, hoarse voice, dizziness, or widespread vomiting develops
conditionalActions.action: Treat immediately as anaphylaxis—use their epinephrine autoinjector if available and call 911 right away.

warnings: Do NOT scratch hives—scratching worsens histamine release and risks skin infection.
Never assume a mild reaction to a known food or sting allergen will stay mild—watch closely for early airway or dizziness signs.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately if breathing changes, voice becomes hoarse, tongue/throat swells, or the person feels dizzy, faint, or unwell
Consult a doctor or pharmacist if mild rash/allergy symptoms persist or affect a young child

learnMore.overview: Mild-to-moderate allergic reactions involve localized skin, eye, or nasal histamine release without airway narrowing or blood-pressure drop. First aid focuses on removing the allergen, soothing symptoms, and watching for escalation to anaphylaxis.
causes: Pollen, dust mites, animal dander, insect bites, cosmetics/detergents, mild food allergies, or medications
riskFactors: Personal or family history of eczema, asthma, hay fever, or food allergies
detailedRecognition: Hives (urticaria) appear as raised, intensely itchy patches that blanch when pressed; unlike anaphylaxis, breathing, swallowing, and blood pressure remain completely normal.
prevention: Identify and avoid known triggers and rinse skin/eyes promptly after outdoor pollen or animal contact.
preparation: Keep sterile saline drops, fragrance-free moisturizer, and prescribed allergy plans accessible.
explanations: Cool compresses and emollients calm skin nerve endings, while oral antihistamines block histamine receptors for comfort (though they cannot stop life-threatening anaphylaxis).
additionalPrecautions: Avoid sedating antihistamines when alertness is needed or when monitoring for worsening symptoms.
followUpCare: See a healthcare provider to identify unknown triggers—especially after any reaction to food, insect venom, or medicine.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 immediately, treat any obvious cause (such as pressing firmly on severe bleeding), lay the person flat on their back, and keep them warm.
recognitionSigns: Pale, grey/ashy (or pale inner eyelids/palms in darker skin), cold, clammy, sweaty skin
Rapid, shallow breathing and fast, weak pulse
Restlessness, anxiety, dizziness, extreme thirst, confusion, or falling alertness
steps: Call 911 immediately—circulatory shock is life-threatening and cannot be reversed without emergency medical care.
Treat any visible cause immediately, such as applying firm direct pressure to severe external bleeding or using epinephrine for anaphylaxis.
Help the person lie flat on their back on an insulated surface (blanket/coat underneath) unless breathing trouble, chest injury, or heart attack requires sitting semi-upright.
Loosen tight clothing around the neck, chest, and waist.
Cover the person with a blanket or coat to prevent heat loss without overheating them.
Give NOTHING to eat, drink, or smoke, reassure them calmly, and monitor breathing and responsiveness continuously until EMS arrives.

conditionalActions.condition: If there is NO evidence of spinal/pelvic/leg trauma or breathing pain and lying flat does not improve dizziness
conditionalActions.action: Temporarily raise the person's legs 30–60 degrees ONLY if it causes zero pain or discomfort; lower them if uncomfortable.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is visibly in late pregnancy
conditionalActions.action: Tilt her gently onto her left side (or place a folded blanket under her right hip) so the uterus does not compress major blood vessels.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes unresponsive
conditionalActions.action: Place in the recovery position if breathing normally, or start CPR immediately if not breathing normally.

warnings: NEVER give water, food, or alcohol even if the person complains of intense thirst—internal surgery may be needed and vomiting risks aspiration.
NEVER apply hot water bottles or direct heat sources to warm someone in shock—surface heat draws blood away from vital organs.
Do NOT raise the legs if head, spine, chest, abdominal, pelvic, or leg injury is suspected.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for all suspected shock—early hospital fluid/blood resuscitation is essential

learnMore.overview: Circulatory shock is life-threatening failure of the cardiovascular system to deliver enough oxygenated blood to vital organs (brain, heart, kidneys). Psychological fright alone is different from medical circulatory shock.
causes: Severe external or internal bleeding, extensive burns, severe dehydration/vomiting/diarrhoea, heart attack, severe infection (sepsis), or anaphylaxis
riskFactors: Delayed bleeding control, cold environment worsening blood clotting, older age, infancy, or blood-thinning medications
detailedRecognition: Early shock causes anxiety, restlessness, fast pulse, and cool extremities; late shock leads to confusion, gasping breathing, extreme pallor/mottling, and unresponsiveness.
prevention: Control severe bleeding immediately, rehydrate early in severe diarrhoea/heat illness, and keep casualties insulated from cold ground.
preparation: Include emergency foil/fleece blankets and trauma dressings in first aid kits.
explanations: Hypothermia impairs blood clotting ('lethal triad' of trauma), so insulating the casualty from cold ground and air directly helps survival.
Passive leg raising (30–60°) produces only a brief (~7 minute) return of venous blood and must never delay bleeding control or cause trauma pain.
additionalPrecautions: Moisten dry lips lightly with a damp cloth if extreme thirst is distressing, without letting them swallow water.
followUpCare: Emergency hospital resuscitation, intravenous fluids/blood products, and definitive treatment of the underlying cause.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: If the person is awake and able to swallow safely, give 15–20 g of fast-acting sugar (glucose tablets, 3 teaspoons of sugar in water, fruit juice, or regular non-diet candy) immediately.
recognitionSigns: Sudden shakiness, sweating, pale skin, hunger, fast heartbeat, or dizziness
Confusion, irritability, slurred speech, clumsiness, or uncharacteristic behaviour (can mimic stroke or intoxication)
Known diabetes, insulin/diabetes medication use, missed meal, or heavy exercise
steps: Help the person sit or lie down safely and confirm they are fully awake and able to swallow.

Give 15–20 g of fast-acting oral glucose immediately: glucose tablets (preferred), OR 150–200 mL fruit juice / regular (non-diet) soda, OR 3 teaspoons (15–20 g) of table sugar dissolved in water, OR regular sugary sweets/jellybeans (smaller 10–15 g portion for young children).
Wait 10–15 minutes while resting and re-check symptoms (and blood glucose if they have their own meter).
Give a second 15–20 g dose of fast-acting sugar if symptoms do not improve after 15 minutes, and call 911 if still unwell.
Offer a longer-acting carbohydrate snack (such as a sandwich, banana, or biscuits) once they feel fully alert and recovered.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is drowsy, unable to swallow safely, seizing, or unresponsive
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 immediately, give NOTHING by mouth, place in the recovery position if breathing normally, and use prescribed emergency glucagon (nasal or injection) ONLY if available and trained.

conditionalActions.condition: If you are unsure whether a diabetic person has LOW or HIGH blood sugar
conditionalActions.action: Treat as LOW blood sugar (hypoglycemia) if awake and able to swallow—a small dose of sugar quickly saves brain function in hypoglycemia and causes minimal harm in high blood sugar.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person cannot swallow but commercial glucose gel is available and local protocol allows buccal use
conditionalActions.action: Prefer calling 911 rather than risking choking; never pour liquids into an unresponsive person's mouth.

warnings: NEVER give food, drink, or glucose tablets by mouth to someone who is drowsy, confused to the point of gagging, seizing, or unresponsive.
NEVER administer insulin as first aid—giving insulin to someone with low blood sugar can be fatal.
Do NOT use 'diet' or sugar-free drinks/candies, and avoid chocolate/fatty foods first because fat slows sugar absorption.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately if the person is unresponsive, seizing, unable to swallow, fails to improve 15 minutes after a second sugar dose, or has signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, severe vomiting/dehydration)

learnMore.overview: Hypoglycemia (blood glucose typically below 3.9 mmol/L or 70 mg/dL) starves the brain of fuel within minutes. Prompt oral glucose rapidly reverses mild-to-moderate episodes, while unresponsiveness is a life-threatening emergency.
causes: Excess insulin or glucose-lowering tablets, delayed or skipped meals, unaccustomed intense exercise, alcohol intake without food, or illness
riskFactors: Type 1 or insulin-treated Type 2 diabetes, young children, older adults, or impaired hypoglycemia awareness
detailedRecognition: Hypoglycemia develops rapidly (minutes), whereas high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) usually develops over hours to days with extreme thirst, frequent urination, nausea, fruity breath, and drowsiness.
prevention: Carry glucose tablets or sugary snacks everywhere, eat regular meals around exercise/alcohol, and wear diabetes identification.
preparation: Know that 15–20 g of glucose equals roughly 4–5 standard 4 g glucose tablets, 1 tablespoon of sugar/honey (honey only if >1 year old), or half a cup (150–200 mL) of regular juice/soda.
explanations: Pure dietary glucose tablets resolve symptoms faster than sucrose/fructose foods, though household sugar, juice, or regular sweets are effective alternatives when tablets are unavailable.
additionalPrecautions: Never give honey to infants under 1 year of age (infant botulism risk).
followUpCare: Advise the person to review insulin/medication doses with their healthcare team after any severe or unexplained episode.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stay calm, clear hard or sharp objects away, cushion the person's head with something soft, time the seizure, and NEVER put anything in their mouth or restrain them.
recognitionSigns: Sudden collapse, body stiffening, and rhythmic jerking of arms, legs, or face
Loss of awareness, staring blankly, noisy breathing, drooling, or loss of bladder/bowel control
Drowsiness, confusion, or deep sleep after shaking stops (post-ictal phase)
steps: Stay with the person, note the exact start time of the seizure, and move furniture, sharp objects, or hazards out of their way.
Place something soft and flat (folded jacket, towel, or your hands) underneath their head and loosen tight clothing/ties around the neck.
Let the seizure run its course WITHOUT holding them down or putting anything at all in their mouth.
Check breathing as soon as jerking stops—if unresponsive and breathing normally, roll them gently onto their side in the recovery position to let saliva/blood drain.
Stay beside them calmly, protect their dignity/privacy from crowds, and reassure them gently until they are fully awake and oriented.

Call 911 immediately if the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, a second seizure starts, it is their first known seizure, or they are injured, pregnant, diabetic, in water, or not breathing normally afterward.

conditionalActions.condition: If a young child (6 months to 5 years) has a febrile seizure with fever
conditionalActions.action: Protect from injury during shaking, remove excess heavy clothing/blankets once safe to cool gently (NEVER use ice baths or cold water sponging), place in recovery position afterward, and seek medical evaluation.

conditionalActions.condition: If the seizure happens in water (pool, bath, or sea)
conditionalActions.action: Support the person's head so their face stays above water, remove them from water once jerking subsides (or immediately if safe), check breathing, and ALWAYS call 911.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person is NOT breathing normally after the seizure stops
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 and start CPR immediately.

warnings: NEVER put spoons, fingers, wallets, cloth, or any object into the person's mouth—they cannot swallow their tongue, and objects break teeth or block the airway.
NEVER restrain or pin down convulsing limbs—restraint causes fractures and muscle tears.
NEVER give water, food, or oral tablets until the person is completely awake and alert.
emergencyEscalation: Seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes or repeated seizures without regaining consciousness between them
First-ever seizure, seizure in water, pregnancy, diabetes, or serious head/body injury
Normal breathing does not resume promptly or consciousness fails to return within 5–10 minutes after shaking stops

learnMore.overview: A seizure is caused by temporary abnormal bursts of electrical activity in the brain. Most generalized tonic-clonic seizures stop naturally within 1–3 minutes; first aid prevents secondary injury and keeps the airway clear afterward.
causes: Epilepsy, rapid fever rise in young children (febrile seizures), head trauma, stroke, low blood sugar, poisoning/alcohol withdrawal, heatstroke, or eclampsia in pregnancy
riskFactors: Missed anti-seizure medication, sleep deprivation, high fever in toddlers, flashing lights (in photosensitive epilepsy), or severe illness
detailedRecognition: Non-convulsive (focal or absence) seizures may cause blank staring, lip-smacking, wandering, or plucking at clothes—guide the person gently away from danger (stairs/traffic) without grabbing abruptly.
prevention: Take prescribed anti-epileptic medications consistently and supervise bath/swimming safety for people with epilepsy.
preparation: Check discreetly for a medical-alert bracelet or personalized seizure action plan.
explanations: Muscles relax deeply right after a convulsion, allowing the tongue, saliva, or vomit to block the airway unless the person is turned onto their side.
additionalPrecautions: Cover the person with a light coat or ask bystanders to step back if urinary incontinence occurred, preserving dignity.
followUpCare: All first-time seizures and febrile seizures in infants/young children require medical evaluation to confirm the underlying cause.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Help the person sit or lie down on the floor immediately to prevent a fall, and guide them through lower-body muscle-tensing manoeuvres if they feel faint.
recognitionSigns: Sudden light-headedness, dizziness, tunnel/blurred vision, or ringing in the ears
Pale, sweaty skin, nausea, or sudden warm/cold feeling after standing, heat, pain, or seeing blood
Brief loss of consciousness lasting seconds to 1–2 minutes with rapid full recovery once lying flat
steps: Help a person who feels faint sit down on the ground or lie flat immediately so they cannot fall and hit their head.

Coach a responsive person with warning signs to use lower-body physical counterpressure manoeuvres: squat down OR cross their legs tightly while tensing leg, buttock, and abdominal muscles firmly for 30–40 seconds.
Ensure fresh air, loosen tight collars or belts, and reassure them calmly.
Check responsiveness and normal breathing immediately if the person actually faints—if unresponsive for more than a moment while breathing normally, roll onto their side in the recovery position.
Keep the person lying down for at least 10 minutes after feeling better, then help them sit up and stand in slow stages—lying flat again immediately if dizziness returns.
Offer small sips of cool water ONLY after they are completely awake, alert, and sitting up comfortably.

conditionalActions.condition: If fainting occurs DURING physical exercise, while lying down, with chest pain/palpitations, or consciousness does NOT return within 1–2 minutes
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 immediately—this may be a dangerous heart rhythm or medical emergency rather than simple fainting.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person stops breathing normally
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 and start CPR immediately.

warnings: Do NOT sit a fainting person upright on a chair with their head forced between their knees—they can pitch forward onto their head and brain blood flow stays low.
Do NOT slap the face, shake them, splash water, or hold smelling salts/ammonia under their nose.
Do NOT use physical counterpressure manoeuvres if chest pain, heart attack, or injury is suspected.
emergencyEscalation: Does not regain full alertness within 1–2 minutes
Fainting during exertion/sports, while lying down, or accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, back/belly pain, or FAST stroke signs
Repeated fainting, older age, pregnancy, heart disease history, or head/body injury from falling

learnMore.overview: Simple fainting (vasovagal or orthostatic syncope) is a brief, temporary drop in blood flow to the brain. Lying flat and tensing large lower-body muscles rapidly pushes venous blood back to the heart and brain, preventing falls and injury.
causes: Prolonged standing in heat, sudden standing up, dehydration, pain, emotional stress, or sight of blood/needles; serious causes include cardiac arrhythmias or internal bleeding
riskFactors: Dehydration, skipping meals, hot crowded rooms, blood-pressure medications, or pregnancy
detailedRecognition: Brief muscle twitches for a few seconds can occur during a simple faint if someone is held upright instead of laid flat, sometimes mistaken for epilepsy.
prevention: Stay hydrated, flex calf muscles periodically when standing in long queues, and rise slowly from bed.
preparation: Practise leg-crossing with leg/buttock/abdominal muscle tensing (preferred over arm-only isometric grip) if prone to vasovagal fainting.
explanations: IFRC guidelines prioritize lower-body physical counterpressure manoeuvres (squatting or leg-crossing with muscle tensing) because large leg and core muscles return far more pooled blood to the heart than upper-body handgrips.
additionalPrecautions: Check for scalp bumps, tongue bites, or wrist injuries if the person fell before you caught them.
followUpCare: Anyone with unexplained, recurrent, or exertion-related fainting needs medical ECG evaluation.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Check temperature with a thermometer (>38 °C / 100.4 °F is fever), encourage frequent fluids and rest in light clothing, use paracetamol only to ease discomfort, and check for urgent red-flag signs.
recognitionSigns: Measured body temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F)
Flushed warm skin, sweating, shivering/chills, headache, body aches, or irritability
Red flags: baby under 3 months, rash that does not fade when pressed, stiff neck, breathing trouble, extreme drowsiness, or seizure
steps: Measure temperature accurately with a digital thermometer (underarm, ear, or oral per age—avoid glass mercury thermometers).
Screen immediately for danger signs (baby <3 months with ≥38 °C, extreme lethargy, non-blanching rash, stiff neck, or difficulty breathing).
Help the person rest in a comfortably cool, ventilated—not draughty—room wearing a single light layer of clothing and a light sheet.
Encourage frequent small drinks of water, oral rehydration solution, diluted juice, or continued breastfeeding/formula for infants to prevent dehydration.
Give age/weight-appropriate paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen ONLY if the person is uncomfortable or distressed by the fever and local rules/contraindications allow.
Monitor alertness, fluid intake, urination, and breathing regularly.

conditionalActions.condition: If the patient is an infant under 3 months old with ANY temperature ≥38 °C (100.4 °F)
conditionalActions.action: Seek urgent medical evaluation immediately—do not give fever medicine first to mask symptoms before a doctor assesses the baby.

conditionalActions.condition: If a young child develops a febrile convulsion
conditionalActions.action: Protect them from injury, never sponge with cold water or restrain, place on their side once shaking stops, and seek medical care.

warnings: Do NOT use cold baths, ice packs, fans blowing directly on bare skin, or rubbing-alcohol sponging—cold triggers shivering that raises core temperature, and alcohol fumes/skin absorption poison children.
Do NOT bundle a feverish person in heavy blankets even if they feel chilly.
NEVER give aspirin to children or adolescents under 16 years (risk of fatal Reye's syndrome).
emergencyEscalation: Any fever ≥38 °C in a baby under 3 months, fever >39 °C in a young child with unwell appearance, or fever in adults >65 years or immunocompromised people
Stiff neck, sensitivity to bright light, confusion, seizure, breathing difficulty, or purple/red rash that does not fade under a clear glass
Signs of severe dehydration (dry mouth, sunken eyes, no wet nappies/urine for >8–12 hours) or fever lasting more than 3 days

learnMore.overview: Fever (>38 °C / 100.4 °F) is a natural immune response that helps the body fight viral or bacterial infections rather than an illness by itself. How unwell, drowsy, or breathless the person acts matters more than the exact thermometer number—except in very young babies.
causes: Respiratory, ear, throat, urinary, or gastrointestinal infections, mosquito-borne illnesses (such as dengue or malaria in endemic regions), or routine post-vaccination response
riskFactors: Infants under 3 months, older adults, weakened immune systems, or endemic tropical infections (dengue—where NSAIDs like ibuprofen/aspirin must be avoided due to bleeding risk)
detailedRecognition: Use the 'glass tumbler test' on any rash with fever: press the side of a clear glass firmly against the spots; if purple/red spots do not fade, call 911 immediately for possible meningococcal sepsis.
prevention: Practise hand hygiene, keep vaccinations up to date, and use mosquito protection in dengue/malaria areas.
preparation: Keep a digital thermometer and weight-dosed paracetamol with a proper measuring syringe in your home kit.
explanations: Antipyretics (paracetamol) improve comfort so a child drinks fluids and rests, though they do not prevent febrile seizures.
In dengue-endemic regions like the Philippines, paracetamol is preferred over ibuprofen or aspirin during acute fever until dengue is ruled out, because NSAIDs increase bleeding risk.
additionalPrecautions: Check medicine labels carefully so you never double-dose paracetamol across cold/flu syrups.
followUpCare: Consult a doctor if fever persists >48–72 hours, recurs, or follows tropical travel.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Screen immediately for emergency red flags (rigid belly, vomiting blood, pregnancy bleeding, chest pain, or shock), help the person rest in a comfortable position, and avoid giving painkillers or food for undiagnosed acute belly pain.
recognitionSigns: Crampy, dull, burning, or sharp pain anywhere in the abdomen or pelvis
Nausea, bloating, vomiting, diarrhoea, or menstrual cramping
Emergency red flags: board-hard/severely tender abdomen, fainting/shock, vomiting blood/coffee-ground material, black/bloody stools, pregnancy pain/bleeding, or pain spreading to chest/shoulder
steps: Check immediately for life-threatening red flags and call 911 if pain is sudden and severe, the belly feels rigid/hard, or signs of shock, bleeding, pregnancy complication, or chest pain are present.
Help the person rest in the position most comfortable for them (often lying down with knees bent, or lying on their right side if mild fullness/discomfort started right after eating).
Provide a clean bowl/bag in case of vomiting and reassure them calmly.

Withhold solid food—and withhold all food, water, and oral painkillers if acute surgical abdominal pain (such as appendicitis) is possible; offer small sips of clear water ONLY for mild uncomplicated indigestion/gastroenteritis.
Monitor pain intensity, temperature, breathing, and alertness closely.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person clearly recognizes their usual uncomplicated menstrual cramps (dysmenorrhea) with no red flags
conditionalActions.action: Apply a warm compress or wrapped heating pad/warm water bottle to the lower abdomen and assist with paracetamol or an NSAID (such as ibuprofen) if local rules permit and not contraindicated.

conditionalActions.condition: If abdominal pain occurs in a woman who is pregnant or could be pregnant (especially one-sided pelvic pain or vaginal bleeding)
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 or seek emergency hospital care immediately for possible ectopic pregnancy or obstetric emergency.

warnings: Do NOT give painkillers, aspirin/NSAIDs, or laxatives for undiagnosed sudden or severe abdominal pain—NSAIDs worsen stomach bleeding, laxatives can rupture an inflamed appendix, and medicines may complicate hospital assessment.
Do NOT apply hot water bottles directly to bare skin or to a suspected surgical abdomen.
emergencyEscalation: Sudden agonizing pain, hard/rigid abdomen, pain worsening on movement/coughing (especially shifting to the lower right belly), or fever >39–40 °C
Vomiting blood/dark 'coffee grounds', black tarry or bloody stools, yellowing skin/eyes (jaundice), or inability to keep fluids down
Abdominal pain in pregnancy, testicular/groin pain, chest/jaw/back radiation, dizziness, or fainting

learnMore.overview: Abdominal pain ranges from harmless trapped wind, indigestion, or menstrual cramps to surgical emergencies such as appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, perforated ulcer, bowel obstruction, or heart attack presenting as upper-stomach pain.
causes: Gastroenteritis, indigestion/reflux, constipation, menstrual cramps, urinary tract infection, kidney/gallbladder stones, appendicitis, or ectopic pregnancy
riskFactors: NSAID overuse, gallstones, pregnancy, older age (where serious conditions like aortic aneurysm or cardiac pain can mimic stomach upset), or contaminated food/water
detailedRecognition: Appendicitis classically starts around the navel before moving to the lower right abdomen with loss of appetite, low fever, and pain on walking or coughing.
prevention: Practise safe food and water hygiene, eat fibre-rich meals, and stay hydrated.
preparation: Keep oral rehydration salts for viral diarrhoea and a reusable heat pack for menstrual cramps.
explanations: Lying on the right side after a heavy meal helps gravity aid stomach emptying in mild post-meal discomfort, whereas bent knees relax tense abdominal wall muscles.
additionalPrecautions: In toddlers and infants, inconsolable crying with knees drawn up to the chest or red 'currant-jelly' stool requires urgent hospital assessment (possible intussusception).
followUpCare: Seek medical evaluation for any unexplained abdominal pain lasting more than 24 hours or recurring.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 / midwife immediately, wash hands thoroughly, ensure a warm clean private space, support the baby gently as it emerges WITHOUT pulling, and dry and place the baby skin-to-skin on the mother's chest.
recognitionSigns: Strong, regular contractions every 2–3 minutes or waters breaking
Mother feels an overwhelming urge to push or feels like having a bowel movement
Baby's head (crowning) is visible at the vaginal opening—birth is imminent and too close to travel safely
steps: Call 911 (and the mother's midwife/doctor) immediately on speakerphone so an operator can guide you.
Protect privacy, keep the room warm, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water (wear clean gloves if available), and lay clean towels/sheets beneath the mother.
Help the mother choose a comfortable position (upright, squatting, kneeling, hands-and-knees, or side-lying; if lying on her back, place a pillow under her right hip so she tilts slightly left).
Support the baby's head gently with clean hands as it emerges naturally—NEVER pull on the baby's head, neck, or shoulders; once shoulders emerge, support the slippery body securely.

Dry the newborn thoroughly right away with a clean warm towel, place the baby skin-to-skin on the mother's bare chest, and cover both mother and baby (including a dry cap/cloth over the baby's head, leaving face clear) with warm dry blankets.

Leave the umbilical cord intact while waiting for EMS (do NOT cut it unless medical help is completely unavailable and sterile tools exist, and ALWAYS wait at least 1 minute—until pulsations stop—in a vigorous baby).

Allow the placenta (afterbirth) to deliver naturally without ever pulling the cord, keep the placenta in a clean bag/bowl for EMS inspection, and encourage breastfeeding or gently massage a soft lower uterus if heavy bleeding occurs.

conditionalActions.condition: If the umbilical cord is wrapped loosely around the baby's neck as the head emerges
conditionalActions.action: Slip one finger gently under the loop to ease it over the baby's head; if too tight, keep the baby close to the mother's thighs as the body delivers so the cord does not tear.

conditionalActions.condition: If the newborn does NOT cry or breathe normally within 30–60 seconds of thorough drying and gentle back rubbing
conditionalActions.action: Place the baby on a firm flat warm surface with head in neutral position, clear visible mouth secretions gently, and start Infant CPR (starting with 5 rescue breaths if trained).

conditionalActions.condition: If the umbilical cord protrudes BEFORE the baby (cord prolapse) or feet/buttocks appear first
conditionalActions.action: Update 911 urgently; for cord prolapse, help the mother into knees-to-chest position (hips high) to take pressure off the cord and never push the cord back inside.

warnings: NEVER ask the mother to cross her legs or hold the baby back.
NEVER pull on the baby during birth and NEVER pull on the umbilical cord to speed up the placenta.
NEVER slap or hold a newborn upside down by the ankles—dry firmly and rub the back gently to stimulate breathing.
Do NOT wash off the white creamy coating (vernix) on the newborn's skin—it protects warmth and immunity.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for all unplanned out-of-hospital births, heavy vaginal bleeding before or after delivery, newborn breathing difficulty, premature labour, breech presentation, or maternal seizures/severe headache

learnMore.overview: Unplanned out-of-hospital childbirth usually progresses naturally without forceful intervention. The first aider's critical priorities are infection prevention (clean hands/surfaces), supporting a gentle unhurried delivery, preventing newborn hypothermia immediately after birth, and watching for maternal bleeding.
causes: Rapid (precipitate) labour, transport delays, disasters, or premature labour
riskFactors: Previous fast deliveries, distance from maternity facilities, or severe weather/disasters blocking roads
detailedRecognition: First-stage labour involves gradually closer contractions; second-stage labour begins with irresistible pushing urges and bulging/crowning at the perineum; third-stage is delivery of the placenta (usually 5–30 minutes after the baby).
prevention: Arrange maternity transport plans early and head to the hospital before contractions become very frequent.
preparation: Gather clean towels, warm blankets, clean plastic bags, soap/gloves, and sanitary pads (never tampons).
explanations: Wet newborns lose body heat four times faster than adults, and hypothermia rapidly worsens breathing and survival—immediate thorough drying and skin-to-skin contact are life-saving.
Waiting at least 60 seconds before cord clamping transfers vital iron-rich placental blood to the newborn, and leaving an uncut cord intact avoids tetanus/infection when EMS is on the way.
additionalPrecautions: If heavy bleeding (>500 mL / soaking pads rapidly) occurs AFTER the placenta delivers, rub the mother's lower abdomen firmly around the navel to help the uterus contract and keep baby skin-to-skin/suckling.
followUpCare: Both mother and newborn require prompt hospital/midwife examination after delivery.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Check immediately that breathing and swallowing saliva are safe (no drooling or noisy breathing), encourage frequent small sips of water or warm soothing drinks, and use paracetamol/ibuprofen for pain if permitted.
recognitionSigns: Painful, scratchy, or burning throat, worse when swallowing
Red swollen tonsils, mild cough, runny nose, or mild fever
Airway emergency red flags: drooling, inability to swallow saliva, muffled 'hot-potato' voice, high-pitched stridor, or sitting upright leaning forward to breathe
steps: Check immediately for airway red flags (drooling, inability to swallow saliva, stridor, or breathing difficulty)—if present, call 911 immediately and do NOT inspect inside the throat.
Encourage regular small sips of cool water or warm soothing drinks (such as warm water with honey ONLY for adults and children over 1 year old) to keep the throat moist.
Offer hard lozenges or ice chips ONLY to adults and older children who have zero choking risk (never to young children).
Assist with paracetamol or ibuprofen for throat pain/fever if local rules permit and not contraindicated (never give aspirin to under-16s).
Help the person rest their voice and avoid cigarette smoke or dry irritants.

conditionalActions.condition: If drooling, muffled voice, severe pain preventing swallowing saliva, or noisy breathing is present
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 immediately, keep the person sitting calmly upright, and never put a spoon or tongue depressor in their mouth (suspected epiglottitis or deep throat abscess).

warnings: NEVER take leftover or unprescribed antibiotics—most sore throats are viral, and unnecessary antibiotics cause resistance and side effects.
NEVER give honey to babies under 1 year old (infant botulism risk) or hard lozenges to children under 4–5 years (choking risk).
NEVER look inside the mouth with an object if a child or adult is drooling and struggling to breathe.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for drooling, inability to swallow liquids/saliva, noisy/difficult breathing, neck swelling, or inability to open the mouth fully
See a doctor if sore throat lasts >5–7 days, has high fever with pus on tonsils and no cough, or occurs in regions/patients at risk of rheumatic fever

learnMore.overview: Most acute sore throats (pharyngitis/tonsillitis) are caused by self-limiting respiratory viruses and resolve within 5–7 days. First aid focuses on hydration, safe pain relief, antibiotic stewardship, and spotting rare life-threatening airway swelling.
causes: Common cold/flu viruses (~80–90%), Group A Streptococcus bacteria ('strep throat'), dry air, smoke irritation, or voice strain
riskFactors: Close school/household contact, tobacco smoke exposure, or incomplete Hib vaccination (for epiglottitis)
detailedRecognition: Viral sore throat usually comes with cough, runny nose, or hoarseness; bacterial strep throat more often causes sudden throat pain, fever, tender neck glands, and tonsil exudate without a cough.
prevention: Wash hands frequently, avoid sharing cups/utensils when ill, and keep routine childhood immunizations up to date.
preparation: Keep paracetamol and a thermometer at home.
explanations: Frequent sips stimulate saliva and coat inflamed throat mucosa, reducing pain spasms.
additionalPrecautions: Warm saltwater gargles can soothe older children and adults who can gargle and spit safely without swallowing.
followUpCare: Medical assessment for persistent symptoms or suspected streptococcal infection requiring a full prescribed antibiotic course.

topics.title: Earache and Foreign Object in the Ear

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Help the person sit upright, apply a warm (or cool) cloth to the OUTSIDE of the ear, give paracetamol/ibuprofen for pain if permitted, and NEVER insert cotton buds, drops, or tools into the ear canal.
recognitionSigns: Sharp, dull, or throbbing pain in one or both ears, muffled hearing, or fullness
In infants/toddlers: pulling or rubbing at the ear, irritability, poor sleep, or fever
Visible fluid, pus, or blood draining from the ear canal, or a known bead/insect inside
steps: Help the person sit propped upright (lying flat increases middle-ear pressure and throbbing pain).
Hold a clean warm damp washcloth (or wrapped cool pack, whichever feels better) gently against the OUTER ear only.
Assist with paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain relief if local rules permit and not contraindicated (never aspirin under age 16).
Wipe away any fluid or pus gently from the outer ear shell ONLY—do NOT plug the ear canal with cotton wool.
Arrange medical evaluation if pain lasts >48 hours, affects a baby under 6 months, or involves ear discharge, high fever, dizziness, swelling behind the ear, or a foreign object.

conditionalActions.condition: If a small bead, toy, or seed is stuck inside the ear canal
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT poke with tweezers or cotton buds and do NOT flush water (seeds swell)—keep calm and have a healthcare professional remove it safely.

conditionalActions.condition: If clear watery or bloody fluid leaks from the ear AFTER a head injury
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 immediately for suspected skull fracture—let it drain freely onto a sterile pad without blocking the ear.

warnings: NEVER insert cotton swabs/buds, hairpins, matchsticks, or fingers into the ear canal—this pushes wax/objects deeper and perforates the eardrum.
NEVER pour oil, herbal drops, or unprescribed ear drops into a painful or discharging ear (dangerous if the eardrum is perforated).
emergencyEscalation: Swelling, redness, or tenderness of the bone right behind the ear (possible mastoiditis), stiff neck, facial weakness, or severe spinning vertigo
Clear/bloody fluid from the ear after trauma (call 911)
Earache in an infant <6 months, pus/blood discharge, foreign object in ear, or pain not improving within 48 hours

learnMore.overview: Earache most commonly arises from middle-ear pressure/infection during a cold (otitis media) or outer-ear canal inflammation after swimming (otitis externa). Most uncomplicated viral middle-ear aches improve within 2–3 days with simple pain relief.
causes: Middle-ear viral/bacterial infection, swimmer's ear, altitude/flight pressure changes, referred jaw/tooth pain, wax impaction, or foreign objects
riskFactors: Young children (shorter Eustachian tubes), bottle-feeding lying flat, passive cigarette smoke, swimming in unclean water, or cotton-bud use
detailedRecognition: Sudden relief of severe throbbing pain followed by sticky discharge often indicates a small eardrum perforation—keep water out of the ear and see a doctor.
prevention: Never clean inside ear canals with cotton buds, dry outer ears gently after swimming, keep children smoke-free, and chew/swallow/suck during aircraft descent.
preparation: Keep age-appropriate paracetamol/ibuprofen in family first aid supplies.
explanations: Sitting upright helps fluid drain down the Eustachian tube from the middle ear to the back of the nose, reducing painful pressure on the eardrum.
additionalPrecautions: Keep the ear completely dry during bathing until a doctor checks any ear discharge.
followUpCare: Medical examination with an otoscope if symptoms persist, discharge occurs, or hearing remains reduced.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Check immediately for danger signs (sudden 'thunderclap' onset, FAST stroke signs, stiff neck/fever/rash, head injury, or late pregnancy), then help the person rest in a quiet darkened room with hydration and simple pain relief if uncomplicated.
recognitionSigns: Tension headache: dull, tight band-like ache across both sides of the forehead/neck
Migraine: throbbing one-sided headache with nausea, vomiting, or sensitivity to light/sound/visual aura
Danger red flags: explosive 'worst-ever' onset within seconds, slurred speech/weakness, stiff neck + fever/rash, confusion, or onset in late pregnancy/postpartum
steps: Screen immediately for red-flag symptoms—if sudden explosive onset, stroke signs (FAST), stiff neck/fever, head trauma, confusion, or pregnancy >20 weeks is present, call 911 immediately.
Help a person with an uncomplicated tension headache or known migraine rest comfortably in a quiet, darkened, cool room.
Place a cool damp cloth or wrapped cold pack across the forehead or back of the neck.
Encourage steady sips of water to correct mild dehydration (unless vomiting repeatedly).

Assist an adult with uncomplicated tension headache or migraine to take a simple analgesic (such as up to 1,000 mg paracetamol or standard-dose ibuprofen/NSAID, or their own prescribed migraine medicine) ONLY if local rules permit and not contraindicated.

conditionalActions.condition: If multiple people in the same indoor space develop headaches, dizziness, or nausea simultaneously
conditionalActions.action: Evacuate everyone into fresh outdoor air immediately and call 911—suspect carbon monoxide poisoning.

conditionalActions.condition: If severe headache occurs after 20 weeks of pregnancy or within weeks after childbirth (especially with blurred vision or swelling)
conditionalActions.action: Seek emergency medical care immediately for possible pre-eclampsia.

warnings: NEVER ignore a sudden 'thunderclap' headache that peaks in seconds to a minute—it may indicate a ruptured brain aneurysm.
NEVER give aspirin to children or adolescents under 16 years.
Avoid taking painkillers more than 2–3 days per week regularly, which triggers medication-overuse ('rebound') headaches.
emergencyEscalation: Sudden explosive ('thunderclap') headache or 'worst headache of life'
Headache with fever, stiff neck, rash, confusion, seizure, vision loss, or any FAST stroke sign (drooping face, arm weakness, speech change)
Headache following a head injury, in pregnancy/postpartum, in someone with cancer/blood thinners, or new headache starting over age 50

learnMore.overview: Primary headaches (tension-type and migraine) account for the vast majority of headaches and respond well to rest, darkness, hydration, and early simple analgesia. First aid's vital role is distinguishing harmless headaches from life-threatening secondary emergencies.
causes: Stress, muscle tension, dehydration, skipped meals, poor sleep, eye strain, migraine triggers, viral illness, or rare emergencies (bleed, meningitis, carbon monoxide, pre-eclampsia)
riskFactors: Dehydration, irregular sleep, excessive caffeine withdrawal, screen glare, or family history of migraine
detailedRecognition: Migraine aura causes temporary zigzag flashing lights, blind spots, or tingling in a hand/lip 15–60 minutes before pain starts; any first-time neurological symptom must be assessed as possible stroke.
prevention: Drink water regularly, take screen breaks, maintain regular sleep/meals, and track migraine triggers.
preparation: Take migraine pain relief early at the start of an attack rather than waiting until severe nausea sets in.
explanations: Darkness, quiet, and forehead cooling calm over-sensitized trigeminal nerve pathways during migraine and tension episodes.
additionalPrecautions: Check blood-pressure and NSAID stomach/kidney/pregnancy contraindications before using ibuprofen.
followUpCare: See a doctor for frequent headaches, waking from sleep with headache, or headaches worsening progressively over weeks.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Reassure the person that brief hiccups are harmless, try gentle breathing or cold-water sipping manoeuvres in older children/adults, and gently burp babies upright without using 'gripe water'.
recognitionSigns: Repeated involuntary diaphragm spasms with a characteristic 'hic' sound as the vocal cords snap shut
No chest pain, breathing distress, or neurological symptoms
steps: Check that there are NO warning signs (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, numbness, balance loss, or difficulty swallowing).

Help an older child or adult sit comfortably and try ONE gentle physical manoeuvre: sip cold water slowly, hold a deep breath briefly for 10–15 seconds, perform a gentle Valsalva manoeuvre (exhale gently against closed nose and mouth for 10 seconds), or swallow 1 teaspoon of dry granulated sugar (if safe and not contraindicated).
Hold a hiccupping infant upright against your shoulder, rub or pat their back gently to burp trapped air, or pause feeding briefly.
Allow the hiccups to settle naturally if simple manoeuvres do not stop them right away.
Advise medical evaluation if hiccups persist continuously for more than 48 hours or interfere with sleeping, eating, or breathing.

conditionalActions.condition: If hiccups occur alongside chest pain, arm/jaw pain, sudden weakness, slurred speech, or loss of balance
conditionalActions.action: Call 911 immediately—rarely, sudden hiccups accompany heart attack or brainstem stroke.

warnings: NEVER give 'gripe water', herbal mixtures, alcohol, or sugar granules to infants—gripe water has no proven benefit and carries choking, alcohol, or contamination risks.
Do NOT use paper-bag rebreathing, eyeball pressure, or frightening/slapping someone, and avoid forceful Valsalva straining in people with heart disease or high eye pressure.
emergencyEscalation: Hiccups lasting longer than 48 hours or causing exhaustion, dehydration, or weight loss
Hiccups accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, vomiting blood, or stroke/neurological signs (call 911)

learnMore.overview: Hiccups (singultus) are involuntary spasms of the diaphragm muscle followed by sudden closure of the vocal cords. Brief bouts after eating or drinking fizzy beverages are benign and self-limiting, especially in newborns and infants.
causes: Eating or drinking too quickly, carbonated drinks, swallowing air, spicy food, sudden temperature change, or excitement
riskFactors: Gastro-oesophageal reflux, gulping feeds in infants, or (in >48-hour persistent cases) nerve irritation, metabolic illness, or medication side effects
detailedRecognition: Ordinary hiccups resolve within minutes; hiccups lasting >48 hours ('persistent hiccups') require a doctor's evaluation to check for reflux, chest, or neurological causes.
prevention: Eat smaller meals slowly, limit fizzy drinks, and burp infants midway through feeds.
preparation: No special equipment needed—reassurance and calm breathing are usually sufficient.
explanations: Brief breath-holding, slow cold-water sipping, or gentle Valsalva mildly increases blood carbon dioxide and stimulates the vagus nerve, resetting the diaphragm reflex arc.
additionalPrecautions: Ensure babies are awake and upright—never feed liquids to stop hiccups while a baby is lying flat.
followUpCare: See a physician if hiccups last >48 hours or recur frequently.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 immediately, move to shade/cool air, remove outer clothing, and start aggressive rapid whole-body cooling RIGHT AWAY ('cool first, transport second' when safe).
recognitionSigns: High body temperature (often >40 °C / 104 °F) WITH brain dysfunction: confusion, slurred speech, irritability, staggering, seizure, or unresponsiveness
Skin is very hot to touch—may be flushed and dry OR heavily sweating (especially during sports/heavy work)
Rapid pounding pulse, fast breathing, headache, or vomiting in hot/humid conditions
steps: Call 911 immediately—heatstroke rapidly damages the brain, heart, liver, and kidneys every minute body temperature stays extreme.
Move the person out of sun/heat into shade or air-conditioning and remove outer clothing, shoes, and sports gear.

Cool rapidly and aggressively RIGHT AWAY: for young/adult exertional heatstroke, immerse from the neck down in cold/ice water (1–26 °C) keeping head and airway safely above water; if immersion is unavailable or the patient is frail/elderly/very young, douse continuously with cold water from a hose/shower, drape cold wet sheets with strong fanning, and pack wrapped ice/cold packs at the neck, armpits, and groin.
Continue active cooling until mental alertness improves or core temperature drops below 39 °C (102.2 °F), stopping if violent shivering starts.
Give NOTHING to drink if the person is confused, drowsy, vomiting, or unresponsive.
Monitor airway, breathing, and responsiveness continuously—place in the recovery position if unresponsive and breathing normally, or start CPR if breathing stops.

conditionalActions.condition: If an athlete or worker has exertional heatstroke and a cold-water immersion tub is on site
conditionalActions.action: Immerse neck-down immediately BEFORE ambulance transport if EMS agrees ('cool first, transport second'), holding their chest/shoulders so their face never goes underwater.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person has a heat-induced seizure
conditionalActions.action: Remove from any water tub immediately (or keep head safely out of water), protect the head, and continue wet-towel/ice-pack cooling.

warnings: NEVER give paracetamol, ibuprofen, or aspirin to lower heatstroke temperature—fever medicines do NOT work in environmental overheating and worsen liver/kidney damage.
NEVER leave an immersed person unattended or allow water near their mouth/nose.
NEVER force fluids into someone with confusion, slurred speech, or drowsiness.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 immediately for ALL suspected heatstroke (any heat illness with confusion, personality change, staggering, fainting, seizure, or temperature ≥40 °C)

learnMore.overview: Heatstroke is the most severe form of hyperthermia, defined by extreme body heat (>40 °C / 104 °F) combined with central nervous system dysfunction. Survival without permanent brain or organ injury depends directly on how many minutes core temperature remains critically elevated—immediate on-scene cooling saves lives.
causes: Classic (non-exertional) heatstroke during heatwaves in older adults, babies, or closed parked cars; exertional heatstroke during intense sports, military, or outdoor labour in heat/humidity
riskFactors: High heat index/humidity, dehydration, Infants/elderly, enclosed vehicles, heavy uniforms/PPE, heart disease, or diuretic/anticholinergic medications
detailedRecognition: Crucial myth correction: sweating does NOT rule out heatstroke! Up to half of exertional heatstroke casualties are still sweating profusely when they collapse.
prevention: Never leave children, elderly adults, or pets in a parked vehicle even for a minute; schedule heavy outdoor sports/work for cooler morning/evening hours with shaded hydration breaks.
preparation: Stage shade tents, cold water, ice towels, or immersion tubs at warm-weather school sports and outdoor events.
explanations: Cold-water immersion (1–26 °C) conducts heat away from skin up to 20 times faster than air, cooling core temperature rapidly; evaporative cold-water dousing + fanning + groin/armpit/neck ice packs is the best alternative when a tub is unavailable.
additionalPrecautions: Stop active immersion once temperature reaches ~38.5–39 °C or mental status clears to avoid overshooting into hypothermia.
followUpCare: Mandatory emergency hospital monitoring of electrolytes, kidney/liver function, and clotting.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stop all physical activity immediately, move the person to a cool shaded or air-conditioned place, cool the skin actively, and give cool water, oral rehydration solution (ORS), or a sports drink to sip if fully alert.
recognitionSigns: Heavy sweating, pale or flushed moist skin, headache, dizziness, weakness, or nausea
Painful muscle spasms in calves, thighs, or abdomen (heat cramps)
Person is FULLY ALERT and oriented (no confusion, slurred speech, or seizures—which would mean heatstroke)
steps: Stop exercise or work immediately and move the person into cool shade or an air-conditioned room.
Help them lie flat (raising legs slightly if dizzy) and loosen or remove excess clothing, hats, and shoes.
Cool the body actively by spraying or sponging skin with cool water while fanning, or applying cool wet cloths to the neck, armpits, and groin.
Give cool water, oral rehydration solution (ORS), or a carbohydrate-electrolyte sports drink to sip slowly ONLY if fully alert and not vomiting.
Stretch and massage painful heat-cramped muscles gently (without forceful jerking) while rehydrating with electrolyte fluids.
Monitor closely for 30–60 minutes—if symptoms worsen, vomiting prevents drinking, or ANY confusion develops, call 911 immediately.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person becomes confused, irritable, drowsy, staggers, or fails to improve within 30 minutes of cooling
conditionalActions.action: Treat immediately as life-threatening heatstroke—call 911 and intensify rapid whole-body cooling.

warnings: Do NOT allow the person to return to sports or hot outdoor work the same day until fully recovered and medically cleared if severe.
Do NOT give salt tablets directly (undiluted salt irritates the stomach and worsens cellular dehydration—use proper ORS or sports drinks instead) and avoid alcohol or high-caffeine drinks.
emergencyEscalation: Any sign of confusion, slurred speech, fainting, or seizure (call 911 for heatstroke)
Persistent vomiting preventing oral fluids, chest pain, or no improvement after 30 minutes of rest and cooling
Heat exhaustion in infants, frail older adults, pregnant women, or people with heart/kidney disease

learnMore.overview: Heat exhaustion results from water and salt depletion during heat exposure or exertion. Unlike heatstroke, brain function remains intact—prompt rest, cooling, and oral fluids prevent progression to fatal heatstroke.
causes: Prolonged heat/humidity exposure, heavy sweating without adequate fluid/electrolyte replacement
riskFactors: Lack of heat acclimatization (first 1–2 weeks of hot weather), dark heavy clothing, fever/gastroenteritis, or poor hydration
detailedRecognition: Body temperature in heat exhaustion is normal or moderately elevated (<40 °C / 104 °F) with normal mental clarity.
prevention: Acclimatize gradually over 7–14 days in hot climates, wear light breathable clothing, and drink before feeling parched.
preparation: Carry clean drinking water and ORS packets during hot-weather school drills, hikes, and sports.
explanations: Sweating loses both water and sodium; carbohydrate-electrolyte solutions (4–9%) or ORS restore plasma volume and relieve heat cramps faster than plain water alone after heavy sweating.
additionalPrecautions: Rest in a cool environment for the remainder of the day.
followUpCare: Medical evaluation if symptoms linger beyond 1 hour or affected a vulnerable person.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Help the person rest in a cool place and give frequent small sips of Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS), clean drinking water, or age-appropriate rehydration fluids—calling 911 if drowsy, shocked, or unable to keep fluids down.
recognitionSigns: Mild–moderate: thirst, dry mouth/lips, dark yellow urine, reduced urination, headache, or tiredness
In infants/children: dry tongue, crying without tears, sunken eyes/soft spot (fontanelle), or no wet diaper for >6–8 hours
Severe dehydration (EMERGENCY): extreme drowsiness/lethargy, confusion, sunken eyes, cold mottled skin, rapid weak pulse, or inability to drink
steps: Check immediately for severe dehydration signs (lethargy, unresponsiveness, shock, or persistent vomiting)—if present, call 911 immediately.
Help a responsive person rest comfortably in a cool environment.

Give Oral Rehydration Solution (WHO ORS packet mixed strictly per label in clean safe water) in frequent small sips (or 1 teaspoon every 1–2 minutes for a vomiting child) for diarrhoea/vomiting or moderate dehydration.

Use clean drinking water (or half-diluted apple juice followed by preferred fluids in children >6 months with mild gastroenteritis, or a 4–9% sports drink for exercise dehydration) if commercial ORS is not needed or unavailable.

Prepare emergency homemade ORS ONLY if commercial ORS packets are unavailable: dissolve 1/2 level teaspoon (~3 g) of table salt + 6 level teaspoons (~18 g) of sugar in 1 litre of clean, safe drinking water—measure accurately and taste-check that it is no saltier than tears.
Continue normal breastfeeding (and age-appropriate feeding once rehydrated) for infants and young children.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person vomits while drinking ORS
conditionalActions.action: Wait 10 minutes, then resume giving much smaller, slower spoonfuls every 1–2 minutes.

conditionalActions.condition: If dehydration is caused by suspected diabetic high-blood-sugar crisis (hyperglycaemia / ketoacidosis)
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT give sugary ORS or sports drinks—offer plain water only if alert and seek urgent medical care.

warnings: NEVER mix infant formula powder with ORS instead of plain safe water, and NEVER dilute or concentrate ORS packets outside package directions—wrong salt ratios cause dangerous brain swelling or salt poisoning.

NEVER give plain water alone in large volumes to babies under 6 months (continue breastmilk/formula + medical advice), and avoid undiluted sugary sodas, energy drinks, caffeine, or alcohol (which worsen osmotic diarrhoea).
NEVER give oral liquids to someone who is drowsy, lethargic, or unresponsive.
emergencyEscalation: Lethargy, confusion, fainting, sunken eyes, skin pinch returning very slowly, or signs of shock (call 911)
Inability to keep any fluids down due to repeated vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, high fever, or severe abdominal pain
Infants under 6 months with diarrhoea/vomiting, or no urine output for >8 hours in children / >12 hours in adults

learnMore.overview: Dehydration occurs when body water and electrolyte losses (from diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, or heavy sweating) exceed intake. Sodium-glucose co-transport in WHO Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) enables the gut to absorb water rapidly even during acute infectious diarrhoea.
causes: Acute gastroenteritis (rotavirus, cholera, foodborne illness), heat exposure, intense exercise, fever, or inadequate fluid access
riskFactors: Infants and young children (higher body-water turnover), frail older adults (blunted thirst), outdoor workers, and disaster/displacement settings
detailedRecognition: Urine colour is a practical guide in older children/adults: pale straw indicates good hydration, whereas dark amber/apple-juice colour signals dehydration.
prevention: Use safe drinking water, handwashing with soap, rotavirus immunization, and regular hydration in hot weather.
preparation: Stock pre-measured WHO low-osmolarity ORS sachets in every home, school, and disaster emergency kit.
explanations: Precise 1:1 glucose-to-sodium transport in the small intestine pulls water into the bloodstream; too much sugar (undiluted soda/juice) pulls water BACK into the bowel and worsens diarrhoea.
additionalPrecautions: Use boiled, filtered, or bottled safe water whenever mixing ORS.
followUpCare: Zinc supplementation (per healthcare advice for children with diarrhoea) and medical review if diarrhoea lasts >2–3 days.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 for all suspected hypothermia, move gently to shelter, insulate underneath and over the body (including the head), replace wet clothes carefully, and handle moderate/severe casualties very gently.
recognitionSigns: Mild hypothermia: uncontrollable shivering, cold pale skin, clumsy fingers, slurred speech, fatigue, or mild confusion

Moderate-to-severe hypothermia (CRITICAL): shivering STOPS, severe confusion/drowsiness, stiff muscles, very slow breathing/pulse, or unresponsiveness (core temperature <32 °C; hypothermia starts <35 °C)
steps: Call 911 immediately for all cases of hypothermia.
Move the person into a warm dry shelter away from wind and rain—keeping a moderate-to-severe casualty horizontal and handling them as gently as possible.
Insulate the person from the cold ground FIRST (mattress, folded blankets, sleeping pad, or cardboard underneath) and cover their head and neck.

Remove wet clothing carefully (cut clothes off rather than pulling limbs in moderate/severe hypothermia), pat skin dry gently without rubbing, and wrap in dry blankets plus a vapour-barrier/foil wrap outside the dry layer.
Give warm, sweet, non-alcoholic, caffeine-free drinks ONLY if the person is mildly hypothermic, shivering, fully alert, and able to swallow safely.

Apply active external trunk warming (wrapped warm water bottles, chemical heat packs separated from bare skin by cloth, or electric/forced-air blanket to the chest, armpits, and upper back—NOT bare skin or extremities alone) if shivering has stopped or hypothermia is moderate/severe, while monitoring breathing closely.

conditionalActions.condition: If the person appears unresponsive with no obvious breathing in severe cold
conditionalActions.action: Check carefully for normal breathing for up to 1 full minute (breathing can be very slow/faint in severe hypothermia); if absent, start CPR immediately and continue without stopping until EMS arrives.

warnings: NEVER rub or massage cold arms or legs, and NEVER place a moderate/severe hypothermia casualty in a hot bath or shower—rough movement or rapid limb warming sends icy blood to the heart and triggers fatal cardiac arrest ('afterdrop' / rescue collapse).
NEVER place unwrapped hot packs directly against cold skin (causes severe burns).
NEVER give alcohol, tobacco, or drinks to anyone drowsy or confused.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 for ALL suspected hypothermia—especially if shivering slows/stops, speech slurs, drowsiness occurs, or the casualty is an infant, elderly person, or drowning survivor

learnMore.overview: Hypothermia occurs when core body temperature falls below 35 °C (95 °F)—not only in snow, but also after typhoon flooding, rain, wind, drownings, trauma blood loss, or indoor cold exposure in babies and older adults.
causes: Cold water immersion, wet windy weather (typhoons/storms), mountain exposure, prolonged immobility after a fall indoors, or trauma
riskFactors: Wet clothing, wind chill, exhaustion, infants, frail older adults, alcohol/drug use (widens skin blood vessels and masks cold awareness), or burns/bleeding
detailedRecognition: Shivering is the body's main heat-generating defence; when energy reserves run out below ~32 °C, shivering stops—a sign of worsening danger, NOT recovery.
prevention: Layer windproof/waterproof clothing, change out of wet clothes promptly after flood/rain exposure, and insulate trauma casualties from cold ground.
preparation: Carry emergency foil/Mylar blankets, dry spare layers, and high-energy snacks in disaster/outdoor kits.
explanations: Cold heart muscle in moderate/severe hypothermia is extremely irritable—rough jostling or standing the person upright can precipitate ventricular fibrillation.
additionalPrecautions: Treat hypothermia BEFORE rewarming localized frostbite whenever both are present.
followUpCare: Hospital core temperature monitoring and controlled rewarming.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Move to warm shelter, treat any hypothermia FIRST, remove rings/tight boots gently, protect frozen skin from rubbing or refreezing, and seek urgent medical care.
recognitionSigns: Frostnip (mild): pale/red, cold, painful/tingling skin on fingers, toes, nose, cheeks, or ears that stays soft
Frostbite (serious): white, waxy, greyish-yellow, or mottled blue-grey skin that feels hard/woody and completely numb
steps: Move out of the cold/wind into warm shelter and check for whole-body hypothermia FIRST (treat hypothermia before frostbite).
Remove wet gloves/socks and slip off rings, watches, or tight boots gently before swelling begins; never walk on frostbitten feet unless survival evacuation leaves no alternative.
Warm mild frostnip gently using body heat (tucking fingers into a warm armpit or cupping warm gloved hands over nose/cheeks—WITHOUT rubbing).

Protect true frostbite and go directly to a hospital if medical care is within 2 hours; ONLY if hospital care is more than 2 hours away AND there is ZERO risk of refreezing, immerse the affected part in circulating warm water checked at 37–39 °C (98.6–102.2 °F) for about 30 minutes until soft and pink/red.
Place clean dry sterile gauze loosely between thawed fingers or toes, wrap loosely in dry sterile dressings, elevate gently to limit swelling, and keep warm.
Offer ibuprofen (or low-dose aspirin in adults if permitted and not contraindicated) for thawing pain and tissue protection, plus warm non-alcoholic drinks if alert.

conditionalActions.condition: If there is ANY chance the thawed hand or foot might freeze again during evacuation
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT rewarm it—refreezing thawed tissue causes catastrophic irreversible tissue destruction.

warnings: NEVER rub frostbitten skin with hands or snow—ice crystals inside cells shred tissue when rubbed.
NEVER warm frozen skin near a campfire, stove, exhaust pipe, radiator, or hairdryer—numb skin burns deeply without feeling heat.
NEVER pop clear or blood-filled frostbite blisters.
emergencyEscalation: Seek urgent hospital care for all frostbite (hard, waxy, numb, blistered, or discoloured skin) or concurrent hypothermia

learnMore.overview: Frostbite occurs when skin and underlying tissues actually freeze below 0 °C, forming intracellular ice crystals and cutting off micro-vessel blood flow in exposed extremities (fingers, toes, nose, ears, cheeks).
causes: Sub-zero ambient temperatures, wind chill, wet clothing/boots, high altitude, or direct skin contact with super-cooled metal, dry ice, or compressed gas
riskFactors: Tight footwear, dehydration, smoking/nicotine (constricts blood vessels), diabetes/vascular disease, alcohol, or altitude
detailedRecognition: Rewarming frostbite causes intense throbbing/burning pain and clear or dark blisters—these signs confirm tissue injury requiring hospital care.
prevention: Wear loose-fitting insulated mittens and dry layered socks, avoid touching bare metal in sub-zero cold, and stay hydrated.
preparation: Use a thermometer (or test with an uninjured elbow if none available) to ensure rewarming water stays strictly at 37–39 °C.
explanations: Ibuprofen reduces inflammatory prostaglandins/thromboxanes released during thawing that otherwise clot tiny blood vessels.
additionalPrecautions: Refresh warm water gently around the edge of the basin (lifting the limb out briefly when adding warm water) so hot water never pours onto numb skin.
followUpCare: Specialist burn/frostbite hospital care, tetanus booster check, and infection monitoring.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: STOP ascending immediately at the first sign of altitude sickness (typically ≥2,400 m / 8,000 ft), rest and hydrate for mild symptoms, and DESCEND IMMEDIATELY with help if symptoms worsen or involve breathlessness at rest or clumsy balance.
recognitionSigns: Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS): throbbing headache PLUS nausea/loss of appetite, fatigue, dizziness, or poor sleep after ascending above ~2,400 m
High-Altitude Cerebral Oedema (HACE — CRITICAL): clumsy staggering walk (ataxia), confusion, drowsiness, or behaviour change
High-Altitude Pulmonary Oedema (HAPE — CRITICAL): breathlessness AT REST, persistent cough (dry or pink frothy sputum), chest tightness, blue lips, or gurgling breathing
steps: Stop ascending immediately—NEVER climb to a higher sleeping altitude while ANY altitude symptoms are present.
Assess urgently for life-threatening HACE (ask them to walk heel-to-toe in a straight line; check mental clarity) and HAPE (check breathing at rest).

Descend immediately by at least 300–1,000 m (1,000–3,300 ft) accompanied by a helper and call mountain rescue/EMS right away if HACE/HAPE signs appear OR if mild AMS worsens or fails to improve after 24 hours of rest.
Keep a HAPE casualty sitting upright and warm with minimal physical exertion during evacuation.
Encourage steady hydration with water, rest, avoidance of alcohol/sedatives, and simple headache relief (paracetamol/ibuprofen) for mild AMS while acclimatizing at the same or lower elevation.
Assist with prescribed altitude medications (such as acetazolamide or dexamethasone) or supplemental oxygen/portable hyperbaric bag ONLY if carried, prescribed, and trained.

conditionalActions.condition: If immediate descent is temporarily impossible during HACE or HAPE due to night storm or terrain
conditionalActions.action: Call emergency mountain rescue, keep the person warm and upright, administer high-flow oxygen if trained/equipped, or use a portable hyperbaric chamber if trained.

warnings: NEVER leave someone with altitude sickness behind alone at camp.
NEVER continue ascending 'just to reach the hut/summit' with headache + nausea, staggering, or rest breathlessness—HACE and HAPE can turn fatal within hours.
NEVER take sleeping pills or alcohol at high altitude—they depress breathing and worsen hypoxia.
emergencyEscalation: Immediate assisted descent + emergency rescue for ANY staggering/confusion (HACE), breathlessness at rest/pink frothy cough (HAPE), or AMS not resolving within 24 hours

learnMore.overview: Above ~2,400 m (8,000 ft), lower barometric pressure reduces oxygen in every breath. Ascending faster than the body acclimatizes causes Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS) and can progress to fatal brain swelling (HACE) or fluid in the lungs (HAPE).
causes: Rapid ascent to ≥2,400 m without gradual acclimatization days
riskFactors: Flying or driving directly to high altitude, fast sleeping-elevation gains (>300–500 m/day above 3,000 m), prior altitude illness, or overexertion/cold (increases HAPE risk)
detailedRecognition: Physical fitness does NOT protect against altitude sickness—fit young climbers who ascend rapidly are often affected.
prevention: Ascend gradually ('climb high, sleep low'), limit sleeping altitude gains above 3,000 m to ≤300–500 m per night, and take a rest night every 3–4 days.
preparation: Consult a travel doctor before rapid high-altitude trips regarding preventive acetazolamide.
explanations: Descending even 300–1,000 m significantly increases atmospheric oxygen pressure, rapidly reversing hypoxic brain and lung fluid leakage.
additionalPrecautions: Protect HAPE casualties from cold exposure—cold raises lung artery pressure and worsens lung fluid.
followUpCare: Hospital evaluation after any HAPE or HACE episode before returning to altitude.

topics.title: Decompression Illness (Diving Emergencies — Trained Oxygen Protocol)

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Call 911 / Coast Guard and Divers Alert Network (DAN: +1-919-684-9111) immediately after any post-dive symptom, keep the diver resting horizontally, and—IF trained and equipped—administer as close to 100% supplemental oxygen as possible.
recognitionSigns: Any unusual symptom within minutes to 24–48 hours after compressed-air/scuba diving (especially rapid ascent or deep/repeated dives)
Deep aching joint/shoulder/elbow pain ('the bends'), mottled/itchy skin rash, or extreme fatigue
Numbness, tingling, weakness/paralysis, dizziness/vertigo, confusion, vision/speech trouble, chest pain, or shortness of breath
steps: Ensure water/boat safety, bring the diver out of the water horizontally if possible, and call 911 / maritime rescue AND a diving medicine hotline (such as DAN `+1-919-684-9111`) immediately for urgent hyperbaric chamber transport.
Help a responsive diver lie flat on their back (or recovery position if nauseated/drowsy), protect from cold or heat, and stop all physical exertion.

[TRAINED RESPONDERS ONLY] Administer high-concentration supplemental oxygen (as close to 100% FiO2 as possible via demand valve or non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min) continuously during first aid and transport.
Give oral non-alcoholic, caffeine-free fluids (water or isotonic drink) ONLY if the diver is fully alert, stable, and able to swallow safely.
Record dive profile details (maximum depth, bottom time, surface intervals, gas mix, ascent problems, and exact symptom onset time) and send the dive computer with the diver to the hospital.
Monitor responsiveness and breathing continuously—if unresponsive and not breathing normally, start full CPR WITH rescue breaths (30:2) immediately.

conditionalActions.condition: If you are an untrained bystander without oxygen equipment
conditionalActions.action: Do NOT attempt unfamiliar oxygen equipment—call 911/DAN immediately, keep the diver lying flat, warm, and calm, and give oral water if fully alert.

conditionalActions.condition: If medical evacuation requires aircraft/helicopter transport
conditionalActions.action: Inform dispatchers that it is a diving injury so low-altitude flight (<300 m / 1,000 ft) or sea-level cabin pressurization is arranged.

warnings: NEVER put a diver back underwater for 'in-water recompression'—it carries extreme risk of drowning, hypothermia, oxygen toxicity, and worsening injury.
NEVER tilt the diver head-down (Trendelenburg position)—lying head-down increases brain swelling.
Do NOT ignore mild post-dive joint aches or tingling, and do NOT fly or ascend to high altitude before diving medical clearance.
emergencyEscalation: Call 911 / Coast Guard / DAN immediately for ANY neurological, joint, skin, or breathing symptom occurring within 48 hours of compressed-gas diving

learnMore.overview: Decompression illness (DCI) encompasses both decompression sickness (dissolved nitrogen bubbles forming in tissues/blood during ascent) and arterial gas embolism (expanding lung gas rupturing into arteries during breath-hold ascent). Definitive treatment is hyperbaric oxygen recompression; immediate 100% surface oxygen by trained responders accelerates nitrogen washout.
causes: Ascending too fast, exceeding no-decompression limits, holding breath while ascending on scuba, or flying/driving over mountains soon after diving
riskFactors: Dehydration, cold water, heavy exertion during/after dives, repetitive multi-day dives, obesity, or patent foramen ovale
detailedRecognition: Arterial gas embolism typically strikes within seconds to 10 minutes of surfacing with stroke-like collapse or chest pain; decompression sickness often appears 15 minutes to 24 hours post-dive.
prevention: Never hold your breath on scuba, ascend slowly with safety stops, stay well hydrated, and wait 12–24+ hours before flying or ascending >300 m.
preparation: Dive boats and dive clubs should carry a checked emergency 100% oxygen unit and trained dive first aiders.
explanations: Breathing near-100% oxygen eliminates inspired nitrogen, creating a steep pressure gradient that shrinks nitrogen bubbles while oxygenating hypoxic tissues.
additionalPrecautions: Check the dive buddy as well—shared dive profiles mean the buddy may also develop symptoms.
followUpCare: Hyperbaric medicine chamber recompression and specialist diving physician clearance before any future diving.

quickInstructions.immediateAction: Stop reading or looking at phone screens, sit in the most stable forward-facing spot, fix gaze on the distant horizon, get cool fresh air, and breathe slowly.
recognitionSigns: Queasy stomach, nausea, or vomiting during car, boat, plane, or ride motion
Cold sweating, pale skin, frequent yawning, excess saliva, or mild dizziness
steps: Stop looking at phones, books, or nearby moving objects immediately.

Move to the steadiest seat available (front passenger seat in a car/bus, mid-ship near water level on a boat, or over the wings on a plane) facing forward, or recline back with head supported and eyes closed.
Look straight ahead toward a fixed point on the distant horizon.
